Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with William "Sonny" Greer
Cassettes 1 and 2

Conducted by Stanley Crouch

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

P R O C E E D I N G S

Interviewing Mr. William 'Sonny' Greer, bon vivant, raconteur, legendary American music drummer, sometimes known as Mr. Empire State Building. Now, for the test of the microphone, Mr. Greer, would you just tell us when and where you were born.
I was born in Long Branch, New Jersey, December 13, 1902.
Okay, let's see how this is picking up. You say you were born in Long Branch, New Jersey, December 13, 1902.
Yes.
How much do you know about your family background before --

My family background. I can remember all of my family. My mother's name was Elizabeth. My father's name was William Alexander. I was named after him but they always called me from the time I remember Son. They would say Son, and then they changed it to Sonny. My mother was a modiste and my father is master electrician for the Pennsylvania Railroad.

I have two sisters and a brother. They have all passed away now, but I remember them very well, and the funny part about it, I became a drummer by purely accident. It was nobody in my family musically inclined. You hear a lot

of guys, they say, oh, my mother was a pianist. My father was this or that, my sister, but that never happened in my family. There was nobody musically inclined in my family. My mother was a very famous modiste, a woman that could copy any kind of clothes, like rich people see a beautiful gown in the paper, they would show it to my mother and she could duplicate it.

My father was a master electrician with his own gang working under him for the Pennsylvania Railroad and my sisters, they -- my youngest sister, Madelyn, she became a very -- a hairdresser and my oldest sister was a housekeeper, you know, for a coffee magnate here in New York. My little brother was just on the scene, comme si, comme sa. You know.

But me, when I was a kid, a teenager, I always liked to make money. I was out to make some kind of money. Well, a dollar was big money then, quarter, dime, I'd run errands for the grocery man. I would even run errands for the Chinaman in my town. I caddied when I was 14 years old, I caddied at a place, Deer Beach Country Club, which was very fashionable. This side of Asbury Park, New Jersey and I was caddying for some people at that time in Newark, New Jersey, biggest brewery in the east, one of the biggest was a brewery called Krueger, Krueger beer. They was very big, very wealthy people. I caddied for their youngest daughter. They grade caddies, you know, first class, second, I was her personal caddy.
So I was still going to school. I was going to

high school in Jersey, Long Branch. High School, still there, so every day we had a big school orchestra about 20 or 30 pieces, violins and everything, for assembly. We had assembly every morning, at class, and they would play them in and play them out and maybe sometime give a little concert so in the meantime, they had a drummer. The worst thing in the band was the drummer, but he was in a lot of my classes.

I had taken languages too and I was one of the good pupils-a German lady named Madam Bruskey, I was one of her good pupils in German. So anyway he was the dumbest guy, this guy, I said, 'how come you don't have to make up no classes.' He said, 'Oh, I got to rehearse,' and he'd get away with it.

So that went on a long time, so in the meantime I lost my job caddying by this incident. One day we was out and I was caddying for this girl. They didn't have them golf carts then were you could roll them -- you had to carry this heavy bag, and so we were on the course, and halfway to the first, to about the seventh or eighth hole in the rough, this -- she couldn't play no golf but she -- just a sport, because at that time when you see somebody on the golf course, they were very wealthy. So she hit the ball and it went into sort of a lake like. She said, 'hey, caddy, get that ball.' So all right, I slip out of my shoes and wade in and get this ball. Getting ready to step in the water, up come a snake

with the ball in his mouth. Now, I'm deathly scared of the snake, you know, so I look at the snake and I look at this broad. I said, no, she said 'what's the matter, get that -- ' she cursed a lot, 'get that so and so ball.' I say 'you want that so and so ball, you go get it.' She looked at me like I lost my mind. Here's this heiress to this fortune, youngest daugher. Plenty of money.

So she say, 'You're through'. So she gave me a little old dollar, got a dollar for walking around 18 holes and that was terrible. The bag weighed a ton, so I left the bag, --she anyway she want-- get it and walked off. So in the meantime, that went on -- I didn't have no job. I lost that job completely.

So in the meantime at Long Branch they used to have the Keith vaudeville acts, come to the theatre for a week. They had a colored act there -- when you were on Keith's Circuit, that was the top of the heap, like the Palace was heaven, the Palace Theatre in New York, but Keith's circuit all they acts, was the fine combed, the best in the world. They had this colored act come to Long Branch to the Main Street theatre, named J. Rosamond Johnson and Company. J. Rosamond Johnson was a hell of a piano player. The drummer's name was Eugene Holland. He was, oh, at that time, I know he was six feet tall, very slim, six feet tall. When you were six feet tall at that time, you were supposed to be a giant, and it's nothing now, but at that time, I'm talking about years ago, but this guy -- so

I went to see them, so this guy, this drummer he fascinated me, oh, he was so sharp, man. He sang, he danced and he played those drums just so nonchalant, effortless, just like falling off a log. I looked at this guy and I had to go back and see him again. They were there for a week.

But in the meantime he liked to play pool. I was a pool shark. I wasn't but 14 years old, I was a pool shark. I run the balls off like you take a whisk broom and brush them off, but this eat, that whole week, he was my turkey. They used to put up-I used to win it. So it got along the third day, he say, kid, -- no, I told him, I say, "I saw your show and it was marvelous," I say, "how did you do all them things? You fascinate me," which he did. He say, "kid, I tell you what, you teach me how to play pool like this. I know I can't learn it in no day or two, but teach me the fundamentals and I'll teach you to how drum." I said, "You got a deal."

So every day for the remaining three days he was there, he would give me two or three hours of the fundamentals, and then I would take him between shows and show him pool, so we got to be very good friends, and heavy, man, he could sing -- this cat could sing like a mockingbird and he did all these things so effortless. He was a picture.
So he showed me the basics and I caught on right away, because I loved it. Right away I fell in love with that. So I took the lessons and I got a lucky break. They were

laying off for a week, didn't have to go back to New York, so I invited him to my house, I said, 'Come on, you just well stay down here at the seashore for a week, and rest and have fun, go bathing, swimming, have some fun.' He said, 'You mean that,' and I said yeah, and my mother was tickled to death. She didn't know I was playing -- learning how to play no drums. My mother loved to cook, my sisters experts, and we'd fatten this turkey up, and I'm still taking them lessons.

Now, after he left and went to New York after he stayed a week with us as our guest, I went to school and I run into my German teacher. I say, 'Hey, Miss Bruskey, I can beat that guy drumming you got in that band. He ain't nothing.' I say, 'I can't beat him.' Now, I'm her star pupil in German language. She said, 'oh, you're kidding.' Said, 'no, I'm serious.' She said, 'I tell you what you do, you give me an audition.'

I said, 'All you got to do is bring the piano player,' had a good white boy, you know, hell of a piano player, so he come down and in the meantime they had an eight-piece band that played all the basketball games, all the affairs around that school, so she come around -- I dropped this thing on her. I went through the whole repertoire, man, like Peggie just showed me. Her mouth flew open, never closed. She said 'You sing.' I say, 'do I sing. Does a mockingbird,' so I could sing. You know, a young kid, had a nice voice, could sing. In fact, the

majority of colored person could sing, that's our heritage, singing and dancing, that is our heritage. Don't let nobody kid you. Rhythm, singing and dancing is our heritage. At this later date, they still ain't caught it. They imitate it but we're the real McCoy. You better believe it.
So I laid it on her, and I was all up on the popular songs. I laid a couple of them on her too. She said, 'you got the job.'
Do you remember what any of the popular songs were that you did at that time?

Who. "Avalon." (Sings) "I lost my heart in Avalon." I didn't sing nothing but a pretty songs. I was a crooner. I didn't sing no sugary boogy song. I sing heavy love songs. I didn't sing none of that bullshit, that stuff, My man done me wrong and "Daddy Daddy, La La.." I sang heavy love songs. I stayed up on them.
What was the name of the drummer, the guy who taught you the drums?
The colored guy.
Yes.

His name was Eugene Holland. Eugene Holland, but his professional name was Peggy. They called him Peggy Holland. Oh, man, he was a -- he was picture. He, so anyway, I did this job with this band, was six white boys and me. Only colored. Now you know I stand out like obvious.

I'm the only soul brother in between all them days. so now we get a gig. We start playing the basketball games and the local dances, all that stuff, but I'm still 15 years old. I couldn't go on a gig in Newark, New Jersey or East Orange, or places like that, big affairs. We had a manager of the band, him and his wife, because we were all kids, they used to chaperone us, you know.

So now we get this gig, at the same golf club, the Deer Country Club, a big affair, so now I get all sharp. My mother keep me sharp because I was only colored around there, keep me sharp. I was all dressed up in my blue suit, my finery, so we go to this Deer Country Club. I had never been in the clubhouse in my life, only on the golf course, but in the meantime, this Miss Krueger, every time she saw me I had a cap on or just a pair of pants or old shirt or something, caddy ing, she had never seen me dressed up.

So now -- I forgot all about her, we're playing this Deer Country Club, all the white boys and me and we had a thing we did -- well, we had one white girl, sang. We used to sing by theirself. I'd sing by myself, and then a couple of them would sing and we had a trio -- two white boys, a white boy, the girl and me. Got up to sing. So now the people coming in to the dance and right on the ringside is this broad, this Miss Krueger. Big party.
Remember now, she never seen me dressed up. So now she come in and we played the first set and I noticed --

you know when someone is staring at you. She stared at me, because I'm the only colored there, with all these white cats. So she looked at me, now, she ain't drunk yet. But something in her mind said, I know him. So she asked the waiter, What's the drummer's name?" The waiter said, "I don't know, miss." This is the first time they played here."

That don't satisfy her. She asked the maître'd, "What's that drummer's name?" He said, "I don't know, miss, I never seen him. This is the first time the boy has played. Are you enjoying it." "Very much", because we could play, see, we could play and sing too. So now she ain't satisfied. She comes up to me and says, "I beg your pardon, but don't I know you?" I say, "I'm very sorry, Miss, but you don't know me. This is the first I've ever been here. You don't know me." "I could swear you look just like a boy that caddied for me." I say, "couldn't be me. I ain't got no brother, he don't caddy for nobody."

Now, she's drinking and she ain't satisfied. If she came up to me once, she came up to me about six times. Now she's real drunk and said, "I know you, so what did I tell her. No, I didn't tell her I didn't have no brother, so the last time she come up, I said, "Oh, you must be the lady my young brother caddied for." I laid that fast one on her. She look at me, she ate it up. She ate that up. Now, she's so drunk and she's so bewildered, I began to feel sorry for her. So the

last time I seen her she cursed me out, told me I was fired so I went -- she (unintelligible) sitting there drinking so I went over to her, I said "I am tired of masquerading", I said, "I used to caddy for you."
I went over to her table. She said, I knew it. She thought I was -------. She told all her friends, all over the place with all her friends, "You see that drummer? he was my caddy."

Chest is way out. so the last thing she say, you got your job back, you be on the first tee tomorrow with my bags. I said, "Lady, I'm very sorry, but I'm a professional, I don't caddy no more. I'm a professional, I don't caddy for nobody."
That's how I started and then man, I don't know. I was playing - some friends of mine, I was playing the Plaza Hotel in Asbury Park for the summer.
You were still a teenager then.

Yeah, about 15 or 16, it's been so many years ago, so I was invited to Washington, D. C. by a group called the Conway Boys, very famous. Three brothers sang. played guitar, so I didn't go that summer. But next summer, they come down every summer to play the season -- we call it the season, you know, from Decoration Day to Labor Day, that was the season. I'm still with the white band, though. I'm right on the scene. I'm stepping now. I done advanced so fast, I'm running over myself. (Laughter)
I advanced so fast, you know, and so anyway, a couple of summers later I accepted a trip to Washington. This

is a weekend, and my first day in Washington, D. C., I'm in the poolroom. They had a pool hall right next to the Howard Theatre in Washington, D. C. 7th and T, still there. I'm playing pool, about 12:00 in the morning, a guy come busting in the poolroom and say, 'Can anybody here play drums?' So I say, I can. He say, well, come on, I got a job, the drummer, his wife, he had to leave town, because his wife -- he's back in the alimony. Guy named Cootie Perkins, went to Canada. He's still there.

So I went in the theatre and they had an all Puerto Rican band except the piano player, he was American. And the leader of the band was a woman from New York named Marie Lucas. She used to play the Lafayette Theatre here on Seventh Ave. famous theatre, and she was director, oh, man, she was (unintell.) so I played, got that job.

Now man, I got that job and I stayed on that job for three years, playing in the pit, but in the meantime they had a little group down in Washington, I forget their names. They played a private club from 11:30 to 1:30, private club, very rich people. I got that job, singing and playing. I'm through at the theatre at ten. So I double, I guess I was the first drummer in Washington to double on jobs at one time. I got that job, and now I'm making money hand over fist. Ain't married, ain't nothing on my mind but my hat.
So anyway, I got that job -- that job lasted a
little while, and in the meantime I met Duke. He wasn't thinking about being no professional musician.
How did you meet him?

You know how guys stand on the corner. He was standing on the corner, him and Claude Hopkins, Toby "Otto" Hardwick, standing on the corner, they was talking some jive, so Toby, he's dead now -- very dear friend. They started talking about New York. He said, "Sonny, can tell you about New York." He's from New York. So I come in there and started that jive talk, that old funny talk, telling them cats about New York, painting a glorious picture about New York, and right away them cats they was on me like white on rice.

I was a charter member then and Duke played piano then, but he had a diploma from the University, from Howard University, commercial illustrator, you know paint them pictures, and he wasn't thinking about becoming no professional. He used to play around at houseparties, and clubs or something like that, but he wasn't playing that no mind. Playing music was the furtherest; but Toby could play, He played saxophone and bass, and he was so small, a lot of times his older brother used to have to carry the bass for him, so he took up saxophone.
We all had a clique together like that, so I got a job. The Conway Boys got a job in Washington at Louie

Thomas' cafe at 9th and R in Washington -- you know anything about Washington. -- 9th and R, Thomas Cafe, and Louie they used to own the Howard Theatre, so they cut me into that. Claude was playing the piano, Sterling Conway was playing the guitar and his wife was singing and her and another girl, and I was playing the drums, making money.

In Washington, D. C. at that time it was illegal to sell whiskey, you know, so all the bootleggers selling that corn whiskey, they come in -- I swear I seen them colored bootleggers come in there and just cover a little round table, seat two or three people, just heap the table full of money and come around, and say, 'Help yourself.' Tell the girls help yourself, we made all kind of money. I'm way up on the hog now. I'm noteriety, but Washington, D. C., let me tell you something, about Washington, D. C.

Washington, D. C., all them pretty girls from all over the country used to go to Howard University, man, a guy We're dirt like me and you, we nothing. We're nothing. If you Wasn't a doctor or some of that crap, or if you wasn't real bad, you ain't got a chance. We'd be too dark for them.

At one time I went to a dance on Murray's Casino on 9th Street. I went there and got all sharp man. I was sharper than a tack then. Everytime you'd see me, I was sharp, and everybody they used to see me in the theatre, and carrying on. playing and showing off and singing. Noteriety, so I go to this dance up at 9th and R, Murray's Casino. I know I'm going

to catch one of those pretty -- so I go over I say, 'pardon me, miss, but may I have this dance.' She looked at me like I was dirt. Said, -- ain't said nothing to me. I went up to two or three more and they'd look at me like I'm dirt. Well, I feel embarrassed, so I swore, I say some day, I'll get even got-damned with these people. I thought they didn't learn to that crap down south or somewhere, but Washington, D. C. was terrible.

You know, so I go my way and have me some fun. I ain't paying anybody no mind. Because I'm way up on the hog, I'm making money. Pockets just laughing. And I wasn't married or nothing like that. I didn't know my wife existed then, anyway, Fats Waller came to town. I had been down there and I stayed down there about -- I had been down there about four years then. So Fats Waller came down there, to play Herdick & Seeman, burlesque house, he had them all over the country. Fats had a band played with the burlesque show, so one day Fats come up to the corner and he seen me, he knew me. He says, 'hey, Sonny, can you get me some musicians, I got to go to New York right away.' I said, 'man, you got me,' I'm tired of Washington then. You got me.
So anyway, he said I need five guys. I said I got them. I got Duke, I got Otto and boy called Arthur Whetsol played trumpet, call him 'Chief', and Elmer Snowden.
MR. : Banjo player.
Yeah, come to New York. Duke say

"You know what you're doing." I say, 'Man, New York's my town, don't worry about it. New York's my town." I knew Willie "the Lion" and Lucky and all them guys, and in the meantime I used to go there and rehearse every Sunday. I belonged to the Clef Club. That was big, that was big like the union is now. We had all the big jobs. / Wanamaker and all them people, had all them jobs. I was the youngest member in the Clef Club. We didn't let a guy like Meyer Davis and them cats be, all them rich people looking for the Clef Club, because every one of them could sing and play, so I joined this thing.

I'm 17 now, and anyway -- wait a minute -- anyway, we come to New York, so me and Duke had a room together. I had an aunt in New York, got a room. I think I was giving her about $3.00 a week. We had adjoining rooms for $3.00 a week, so me and Duke had adjoining rooms. Duke ain't never been to no New York. He ain't never seen no building as tall as that in his life.

So man, I told him -- cut that -- (Recording interruption) So now we're in New York and we're just gigging, nothing steady, so we get a job -- Wilbur Sweatman, he was vaudeville, he played three clarinets at one time, but he used a piano and a trumpet and drums. So he had this engagement at the Lafayette Theatre and so I got that gig for us. I got that for us, we played around New York, in New Jersey

but he worked on Keith's Circuit too, but it was just four of us on the stage and him and he played clarinet, three of them at one time. Beautiful. Stage setting, he had a beautiful stage setting, whole lot of drapes, but we used to have to get to the theatre an hour before showtime to get made up.

Boy, when we come on that stage, we waslight as a sheet of newspaper, ain't no way in the world you could tell us. Everybody was light -- like Willie Bryant -- did you ever see Willie Bryant, no. He used to be at that Apollo, He looked like a /white boy, light as Tizol. You saw Tizol.

So that's there, he had an engagement in Chicago or somewhere, but we wouldn't go. Said no, we ain't leaving New York, so he got somebody else, so in the meantime, it's summertime now, a person called Bricktop. You heard of Bricktop.
: Yeah.

Bricktop was working at Baron Wilkins up at Harlem, very famous Negro nightclub, so -- her name is Ada Bricktop, so I was standing on 7th one day, I had met her and knew her, she said, 'Hey, Sonny, I got a job for you all'. I said, fine. She said 'Baron's down at the basement club.' So we went in Baron's and everything we played was so close together but the other little small bands, they just played hurdy, gurdy, they wasn't together -- they never heard nobody

that played like us. Our six pieces sounded like twelve, and we played so smooth -- we were never loud, very soft, beautiful. We go down there in July and stayed the whole summer and one day, it was a man named Hopper, he produced the colored shows and he was producing a show -- what's the name of it, I stayed there four years. Down at 49th and Broadway, what is the name of that club.
Was it the Kentucky Club?

Kentucky, that's the club. Kentucky Club, right on the corner of 49th and Broadway, Howard Johnson or somebody's got it now, down in the basement. This is prohibition, you know, 20's, 1921. I think it was '21 or something like that. So anyway we went down there, they had the floor show, the floor show, Dennis Hopper put on the show, had a comedian, Johnny Hodgins and Joe Smith played trumpet for him. We had a white master of ceremonies, he played piano, and had a white lady that sang, sang opera and all that crap. High tone. And a guy named Burt, he knew a thousand songs. Any song you'd name, he knew it, he'd play it.

But they would go on between the shows. Now, we played down there, and the word spread there's a different band in town. They sound different. Paul Whiteman was playing around the corner, had his band around the corner at the place there. Up the street was the Roseland Ballroom, Fletcher and them up there, all activities right around there, so

anyway at night those guys would get off early. We didn't go to work till 11:00 and we stayed open till 7:00 in the morning, anyway, our club was a little small place and after 3:00 in the morning you couldn't get a seat. They'd stand around and it got so popular, we were packed and jammed. Paul Whiteman would bring all his friends and band down there. But it was so small, a lot of times the guys would want to sit in and play with the band, but they had to sit on the floor. The floor was so crowded you couldn't dance.
The Club Kentucky was something and the money flying. Money is flying. Partner, the money is flying. You believe it. Now that's the 20's when a dollar was a dollar. Ain't nothing now.
We had all the gangsters, all the big gangsters you read about. Some -- he got killed.
Legs Diamond.
Legs Diamond.
Lucky Luciano.
Yeah, and all the Brooklyn gang, they'd rendevous.
At the Kentucky Club.

You'd hear a colored boy named Slim upstairs and that's when the Revenue men were breaking down the doors, you know, because we was selling whiskey. We sold everybody, but couldn't nobody get to drink in my club unless

I give the okay, because we had a boss named Leo Bernstein, he'd come over and say, anybody want a drink. He'd say to me, you know that guy, and I'd say yeah, he's all right. Never got busted. I had a good memory. I could remember all that time, we had six hostesses, you know, just sit around with the stags.. Of course, they gig afterwards. (Laughter)

So now Fats Waller is playing the piano for this guy. Fats got a gig down there playing piano for this guy. Fats had a little piano, first one I saw, one of them little teeney pianos, so between shows Fats and this cat to sing, to take that little piano and go around the room and I see all that money going to that cat, and I say, 'Hey, Duke, why don't we do that?' Making all that money. Why don't you do that. I ain't going to lug no piano.

So this white guy, he got sick or something and he had to lay off, so Fats come in, I told him, I say, 'Hey Fats, I sing, why don't I make the money with you?' So he said, 'Come on, Sonny, come on,' man we went out there and made so much money. I forgot about playing with the band.

What I did, I kept it. Now, the boss, Leo Bernstein he belonged to the syndicate, but he would get drunk off that whiskey every night, and soon as I spy him and he real drunk, I tell Fats, 'play 'My Buddy'.' That was his torch. I'd sing that for him, 'My Buddy,' and man, he would cry and want to give me the cash register. He was my prize turkey.

I stayed down there-- we got so popular, the guys the gangsters bought the Cotton Club, they said, 'I want that band.' What you going to say, when they say I want something they get it. When they told Duke we got to augment the band, make the band larger and go to the Cotton Club, I said man, 'I ain't going up there,' and he said come on. I said I ain't going. I ain't going, so I told Leo I'm going to stay here, let them go, and he said, 'No, you better go.' Because he know. 'I will miss you guys, but you go ahead.'

So I went up there and I wasn't -- it was all right, so when I got up there, it was a big place and the Cotton Club was the rage then. If you come to New York and didn't go to the Cotton Club, you wasn't nowhere, so I went up there and so now, in the meantime, I was the drum designer for a company out of Elkhart, Indiana called Lezy Drum Manufacturing, one of the biggest.
How did you get to start designing the drums?

That's when I started. A fellow, one of the executives of the club come to New York and seen me playing at the Kentucky Club. He said, 'Sonny, how would you like to work for us?' I said, 'What doing?' He said, 'designing, and using all our advance products.' I said, 'all right.' I say, 'well, send me a set.' Well, they sent me five trunks of drums. Vibraphones, everything. The picture's up there on the wall. So I come in the

had that stuff! Cotton Club. Ain't no drummer Nothing! They still ain't got it! All this stuff come, five trunks of it. I sit on the bandstand and they sparkle like -- and man when them gangsters saw that, they say, My God, and when a guy want to get a job in a cabaret, the man say 'You got drums like Sonny,' and the guy say, 'You must be crazy, that drum set cost me $3,000 -- didn't cost me nothing, they sent it, but they don't know that.
Now, I'm going to sit behind $3,000.00 worth of drums. I didn't have to play them. All I had to do was look pretty. Get Jo Jones to tell you some time.

Jimmy Crawford told me that when he went into the Cotton Club when Lunceford was there, that was the first thing, you cannot work in here if you ain't got that stuff, so he had to go out there and get ahold of stuff.

Now, at that time, let's just fill in, before we go on because now we're up to the Cotton Club, but what kind of equipment had you used before then? I got photographs of you -- hold it a moment. (Recording interruption) Bass drum, snare drum, high hat, two tom toms, two 16-inch tom toms on the floor and two medium sized, up top on the bass drum.
That's what you used --
That's what I used then. That's all I used now when I played little quick gigs.
Now, before you -- before about
1930, you were using the smaller set then, because that photograph we just looked at you had a big bass drum, one cymbal.
I said :/ Before 1930.

If you didn't make the scene, because all the faces would come down, all the musicians, white ones, all of them, Tommy Dorsey, Jimmy and all of them, the whole crowd. Red Nichols, all of them. Red Nichols played down the corner from us, from the Kentucky Club.

They would come up to Harlem and hang out all the joints, to steal, see what the cats was putting out. Yeah.

They immortalize this guy. You couldn't put Bix Beiderbecke on a bandstand if you had a derrick and lift him up there. When them cats, when all them trumpet players got to playing, what can you do. He stopped -- tear him up (unintelligible) He was a good friend of mine, Bix was, because everytime we went to Davenport, I would go out to see his people. I hear 'em talk about this guy and that guy, it's a living joke man. It's a masquerade, because you don't have to go hunting for them. You could walk by a little old dive, and hear the damndest music and singing you ever heard in your life. You know what I'm talking about.

These cats -- they don't do nothing. You get one of those chicks, with the $3.00 hair, get a $3.00 guitar and she go out and sing the water's wet, the wind is blowing and right away I see a guy like Merv Griffin, Mike Douglas and

them guys, how many gold records you got. I got 15, 20. They must be giving them away like handbills. They couldn't have made Major Bowes' Amateur Hour. They don't know when the music start, by the colored. They ain't saying nothing. It was put up or shut up. You either had it or you didn't have it. If you didn't have it, you just move aside.

Wasn't no in between, because these people know no talent, as I said, music is our heritage, dancing. Music and dancing, ain't picking no cotton, our heritage. Rhythm is our heritage. You understand what I mean, all them people singing. They caught it from Negro churches. They don't know nothing about that.
They kill me when they talk about man, I'm singing some soul. SHIT.

When you -- do you remember --

No. No, that never come up. What did

come up, the real truth about it, we played -- I don't know how it originated or nothing like that, but somebody -- I don't know whether it was Paul Whiteman because he idolized Duke or Gershwin. He was a steady customer at the Cotton Club.

They used to -- of the things in awe, Duke used to do, so they were sitting up at the Cotton Club and George Gershwin said to Paul, I know what that is, that's jungle music. And it stuck with us. Stuck with us. But never, never, they would never say that because a lot of the guys up there, they may say you guys but they was scared to offend a guy's feelings, and you know, with all respect, the jungle music, and that latched on to us.

Because our first theme song was -- what the hell is the name of that thing, the prettiest one, long before "A-Train." That was the prettiest, "East St. Louis Toodle-oo." Bubber Miley named it that. That was the prettiest theme song we ever had. "A-Train," with all due respect, couldn't even play in the same place with it. We had -- I played chimes all the way through, cathedral chimes and the band was low down growling, real low down, low, low, way down near the bottom. So.... Jungle music.

When we stopped playing that for our theme song, that thing broke my heart. That was the prettiest thing and we used to play it. We broadcast -- we used to broadcast from the Cotton Club from 6:00 to 7:00, every night. We had three of the best announcers. We had Ted Husing, Dick Brokenshire

and David (unintelligible). Three of the best announcers in the business, in the world. They would come up to the Cotton Club especially Ted Husing, he's still living. Like you make out a program, you know, different numbers you want to play. He wouldn't let us. He would say you play this, and he would pick out some of our finest. That's right.
Did you read much when you were in the band?
Yeah.

No. He had what we call a skeleton, had a skeleton, you know, for my part. Just a skeleton. But he let me use my own imagination. He never wrote a part for me. He'd give me a skeleton, and I would rehearse it and I would insert my ideas, like individual solos for the different guys in the band, he never wrote them out.

That's why today those guys are laying in his grave -- they haven't caught us in 25 to 30 years, because it ain't down. Just the basis, and when it comes to a solo and ensembles he wrote those, or have an arranger do it for him, but he knew what he wanted, but like he'd tell Johnny, Tricky, or any of the guys, Lawrence Brown, Tizol, he'd leave it blank. The only thing he'd write, how many choruses he wanted them to play. That's why Johnny Hodges, Carney, there's no more Johnny Hodges, there's no more Harry Carney's -- With due

exaggeration, Lawrence Brown was the greatest trombone player I ever heard in my life. Lawrence Brown, you remember Lawrence Brown trying to make -- well, they were always looking for a ofay--- king --/today in prizefighting, but anyway Lawrence Brown, I know one time on a recording session, if Barney Bigard, on clarinet, if he didn't show or was late for the recording, he would give Lawrence Brown a clarinet part. Ever heard of that, a trombone player playing a clarinet part?

And he would run it clean as a whistle. We were in California making a picture and Tommy Dorsey, he said to me, I'll never forget said 'That's the greatest trombone player in the world.' And Lawrence Brown didn't know what he could do, you better believe it. Barney, and a bass player -- Charlie Mingus just died.
Yeah, I know.
He played with us. He was a hard character to get along with.
Why was that?

I don't know. Temperament. I got along beautifully with him, but he wasn't good for a bunch of guy's organization because he would create a lot of little disturbances. He wasn't -- and the thing about Duke's band we had a band of individual stars. They could stand on their own. On their own two feet, but as a team, they were just like this. My job with the Duke Ellington band, I didn't go

and things. in for all them Buddy Rich solos/. My job was to hold at that level, because you take a band today, they'll start up playing down here and when they wind up, they're playing up here, so fast. Notice it, just notice it. Not that they want to do it.

But invariably they'll accelarate, every one of them, all of them, and we had a band of all-stars. The way they started off, that's the way they end. That was the thing, (Laughter) my job was to keep them turkeys. I didn't want no drum solo, I could imitate anybody. I could do it, but I know it wasn't no good for the band.

Like the guys now, they have no consideration for vocalists. I hear it on the programs playing the big TV shows. The goddamn band played louder than the singer. No good. Because my teacher always told me, when you can't hear the vocalist or hear the soloist you're playing too loud. That's all she said. Anytime you can't hear what the vocalist is doing or hear what the solist is doing, you're playing too loud.

You know what else she said. She died when she was 90-some years old. The last time I saw her, I played at the Hollywood Bowl in California and she was 90-some years old, and she come back, this old lady and she told all her friends, 'That's one of my pupils', hugged me and kissed me and cried.
You know a funny thing, not to be sentimental, my whole career as a professional, my mother never heard me play.

My father never heard me play. My sisters never heard me play. My brother heard me play once. And I played all over the world. There's one thing I regret, my mother could never seem me in action. She kept up with what I was doing and was very proud, but to actually see me play. No. Never saw me play.
Why is that?
We never played -- we played everywhere--
You all never played in --
Never played Long Branch. Never.

Oh, a lot of the boys have been down to my house to visit, but my mother never saw me play. Never. That's one thing that always stuck. You know, parents like to see their kids. Never. They heard about me because I was a notorious character. But they never saw me in action.
(Laughter)

Another thing my teacher told me, she told me don't you ever forget it. She say, "Sonny, appearance is half the battle. When you look good, don't -- that's half of the battle. I had a cymbal -- They had a band called the California Ramblers, a big white band, and the drummer was Stanley somebody. They were a good band, they could play, big band, so we had a fire. you all take your horns home, we're going to have an accident down there tonight. Sonny, leave them drums just like they are." I'd take the cymbals and put them in the piano and pull the lid down, because cymbals ain't going to burn. Man, now remember this is on 49th and Broadway. Man, that morning we get off and go across the street, next to Jack Dempsey's hang out there and drink before we go to Harlem, I was standing up there drinking with some boys in our gang, and get to lollygagging, here come the fire engines, the hook and ladder, there my drum sitting up on the ladder. Sitting up on the hook and ladder.

I swear before God, I ain't exaggerating and lying, that was New York. See, business would get slack. What do you call that. Sort of a two-three week holiday, slow or something like that, we'd have a fire over there. Next day, the insurance people would be rebuilding the club and the boss would tell me, "Sonny, go get a new set of drums."

So I take the cymbal out there and it be all smoked up, and I get me a ten-cent can of brass polish and shine it, sparkle -- this guy with the California Rambler, he would come in there and say, 'hey, Sonny, how your cymbals?' I said, 'Man, that's a gold cymbal, what are you talking about.' Shine, you know. 'That's a gold cymbal.' He say, 'You want to sell it?' I'd say, 'oh, no man, I couldn't sell it. It's a gold cymbal. I won't sell it.' Say, 'sell it to me man, he'd give me 25 or 30
"Go on, you're my buddy, dollars, I'd say, go on and take it." I'd borrow one from the drum store and write to the factory, they'd send me a couple more. Cost nothing.

But that's just you know, you're thinking fast. Think fast. I know when me and Fats was singing, come around on the floor, I used to sing "My Buddy" and all them popular songs. One night feeling good, I sang a couple of risqué songs. Oh, so man I come out and the hostess is sitting there and them drunks, they loved it. Man, money just flying and the cat -- one cat wanted to give me a couple dollars.. The hostess say, "What's Sonny going to do with - two dollars don't give him two dollars. he's going to make it anyhow. Give him five or ten. What's the matter with you."
He didn't want to be showed up. He come over to me. (Unintelligible) they looking out for me. Looking out for little brothers. Looking out for the bruz....(Laughter)
(Laughter)

small band. One night Bubber Miley and Bechet and Toby they wanted to go -- I forget where in Massachusetts, it cost $35.00 one way in a cab. Them cats got drunk up there and kept the cab driver. The bill was a hundred and some dollars. They ain't got the money. Kept him up there all night with the whorehouse,kept him up there all night, brought him back so Charlie Schribman had all the big bands up there. He paid, so the cabdriver had such a good time he give Bechet half the money back.
Them cats took him up there, got him drunk and in the whorehouse and everything. Man, it was just one of them things, man.

Bechet played with us, he played at the Cotton Club too. We enlarged the band. Toby, Bechet, Johnny Hodges, Carney, he stayed with us so then he wanted to go to Europe so he went to Europe and stayed.
But he got along well with everybody in the band?

Beautiful. Beautiful. Beautiful man. Bechet was -- everybody loved him. Even Duke loved him. He was just a funloving man. He lived. He lived. He was beautiful. In fact, all the whole band was beautiful. A bunch of guys that could play, stars, and they was a family. They were a family, please believe me. It was one for all and all for one and Duke was right in=the middle of them. I remember this, reminisce
all of them are gone now, I'm the only one around of the originals, and I don't generally talk about it, bring back too many memories, you know.

And I'm not a sentimentalist. But I recall the many pleasant moments we had together. That's why when a guy, somebody come up to me, I was playing a school, a college and a guy say, so and so and so and so, and some guy, smart guy, uh, only thing I say to him, 'I was there.' That's all I had to say. 'I was there, pal.' You just quoting something to me maybe you read. I was there.' That take care of all that. I was there. That's right.
I remember when I stopped -- I was playing -- I went down to a club in New York here, 62nd Street and 1st Avenue, called Gregory's -- you never been there.
Yeah, I used to come in there and see you all the time.

I used to run across that all the time, you know. Run across different -- you know, white people curious all the time, and I get a kick out of it, laugh, you know. They ask me different things. You know, especially school kids. I tell them something, they brush them off, not impolite, I say, Well some friends of mine are leaving for Chicago. I got to go and tell them goodnight. That's the whiskbroom. I call it the whiskbroom, and they're happy. That's right.
How did -- did the Negro musicians
and white musicians were they very close to each other in those days?

Oh, yeah. You know, because the Negro musicians, those days, they were gods to the white boys, because they were seeking knowledge and things, and the only way they could get it was from the Negro musicians. They were gods. Everytime you turn around you see one of them. They still are gods, to those in the know, because I could name for a week them guys, like Bird, Young, Yard Bird, and Lester Young and of them passed on, all them guys, a lot Sidney and Jabbo, Louis.

What kind of guys -- how did his band sound.

I don't know. Well, you know how them New Orleans bands sound. They sound like ordinary jazz band. You know the Dixieland Jazz Band, they sounded like that a little fuller, because they had more guys. But I tell you

the truth, I never heard a solid band. Duke and them heard them, went up there because they played at the Savoy, but when I left the bandstand, music out of my mind. I didn't try to hear no band. "Man, let's go chase so and so." I ain't got no time. I was looking at making me some money, I ain't got the time to hear nobody play no music.

No way, even guys say come on let's go hear so and so. I heard them all. I visit guys. I never evade them, I always visit guys I like, because we hung out together. We hung out. I know they could play or people wouldn't go hear them. But we got on the bandstand, we was gone.

Zutty, well, Zutty was one of my best pals. Good drummer. Baby, good drummer. Good drummer. beautiful drummer. Sidney Catlett, /Chick Webb, beautiful drumer. Kaiser was a beautiful drummer. He fitted Fletcher's band like a glove. He used to tell everybody he was my brother.

I don't know.
You have a very unusual way of playing. A lot of times......
I can't truthfully say how I developed
my style. As I told you, I always got a lead sheet, a guide, and most of the things I do it was just intuition, like guys playing piano, things come to them. All right.
How can I say that. I used to love to go to the Capital Theatre and hear the symphony band play, because them guys are crack musicians. That was before the talkies, you know.

New York. Capitol Theatre. 50th Street and Broad. Big', and me and Duke used to go there to hear them play. To hell with the pictures, just to hear them guys play. That rhythm section, they was something. And the drummer, I forget his name, he used to do some things, man, so tricky, I would go see him 50 times and then I'd go on the job, I would fool around until I caughtit my way. Same sound, but my idea, me. I would do that all the time. I ain't never told the guy show me how to do nothing. I go and sit and look at him. So when I come off the stage, he say, 'Sonny, why don't you talk back to her, during her numbers like you used to do with Ethel Waters at the Cotton Club.' He look at me like I'm crazy. And we washed everybody away. I used to tell them guys, all them guys supposed to be funny, comedians, you better get all the laughs you can because

from every night, /6:00 to 7:00. The world was waiting for that. Everybody was waiting for that from New York to California and coast to coast, was waiting for that. Well, the way we played. The way we looked and the class we had. They never seen nobody like us. They had heard different colored aggregations that come through on a little ragged-ass bus or something like that, but we would we were the first band and the only band, white or colored, we traveled, we had our own Pullman car, had our own baggage car, and when we was traveling, we had full possession of the diner, because we had certain time to go in the diner, after people -- we wouldn't go when a whole lot of people, because nobody could come in our Pullman car because the door stayed locked, because people autographing annoy you, you know. We

had our own pullman car, with our name on it, our own baggage car, because we traveled heavy. We were traveling heavy. We had own lighting equipment, own stage -- one of the first bands to use a roll down stage and roll back, we carried that, and we carried our own lighting system. One of the first bands with all of them overhead pinpoint lights. Electrician. They never seen that.

They may have seen the colored band pull up in a bus or something but when we pull up we pull up in the station. We never had to run to get no rooms, we paid an extra fare to have our car parked in the station. We had own own pullman porter, and conductor. We had it. That's the way Irving Mills made us travel.

And if we done four or five shows a day in a theatre, you know, every show we had different uniform on. We never wore the same uniform, that same day. Every show we would dress different, different uniforms, from top to bottom. They had never seen nobody like that.

Now we went south, a lot of them cats down south, you know, in order -- confliction, we had the colored over this side, like you know, segregation. We pull up, baggage car in the yard and pay extra to park it. We didn't have to go through that junk. Our guys in the morning, when we get up, we didn't even have to dress. We'd keep on our pajamas and robes and stay in our car, relax all day until the time to

go to work. And if wanted'something in the morning, he would go up and put the order in and have the guy deliver it to us, like we were standing still. I never went nowhere where the guy would tell me you got to go over here and then when we went to the gig, we have a fleet of them cabs wait there to take us, bring us and the average one of them crackers down south, they had never been inside a Pullman car, never saw it, and them porters used to put on the dog, them cats would put on them beautiful starched uniforms and the step to come down, they would lay it. They were actors too. They would act down.

They never seen that. They would come down out of curiosity. Ofays and everybody would come down, we were traveling like kings. That's how Irving Mills had us travel, and when we would come in the theatre and lay it on, that was it. You can believe it. Duke is dead now, the majority of the guys is dead now. But at that time, we were 25 years ahead of all the bands. They never caught us, even today in 1979. Nobody ever caught our band. Nobody's band ever cut our band,know what I mean, outplayed our band.

We were a living legend, we are today. Every tick of the clock, baby, right now and them guys are dead and gone, every tick of the clock, 24 hours a day, somewhere in the world, not only United States, all over the world, somewhere in the world, they are playing some of our tunes. Russia, everywhere else, they're playing some of our tunes. Everytime

you heard Sophisticated Lady." They play "Mood Indigo" damn near as much as they play the "Star Spangled Banner". Yeah, they play our tunes every tick of the clock. That's no exaggeration. Every tick of the clock. They are playing our tunes somewhere in the world, 24 hours a day.

Sensation. That's the first time we really played what you call a stage production, we had

a natural Broadway show like these shows on Broadway nowadays, ain't nothing. They ain't nothing. Them girls stopped the show. Oh, just the girls, the chorus. Stopped them cold. we went to Europe in 1933, he laughed about it. He had been here and made some pictures, but we played his American debut. That's right. We had a lot of firsts.

Now, all American actors, the Palace Theatre, all them bigtime celebrity actors, the Palace Theatre was heaven, that was their heaven. We played it, first band to play it. So Duke don't ask him about no money. Duke say all right, so we give him a lift. Closing night that cat didn't say nothing. 'Thank you, guys,' and didn't say nothing about no money. So that's all right, so we went to California to make a picture. Out there making a picture with Mae West, 'Belle of the Nineties,' maybe you seen it. So he happened to say it, and I said, yeah, --
(Recording interruption)
