Liked us, the stars?
When you all were out there making a movie.

Man, we had a whole dressing room -- place, a stage, where we rehearse our part for the picture, man, them actors got a break, the whole -- where we were playing; it was heaven. All of them was -- wherever we played -- heaven, man, and they would come over and say 'Hey, Sonny, play -- Duke, play your original compositions.' We would. We would have a jam session and every time we got a break, the place was full of guest and visitors, and they stayed so long and the man had to come there and say, 'Stop playing so them actors can get back over there on the set and do their thing.'
How long were you all out there, the first picture.
Oh, we stayed in California, making pictures, about three months. Then we come back east and we'd come back east -- we'd go to California every year and if we
didn't make a picture we'd go on a theatre tour, you know. We played all the theatres in California, San Francisco, everywhere.
Now, when you were playing out in California you -- there -- you didn't have to be -- you weren't bothered with the segregated policies were you.

Oh, no, California was heaven. They never lowered the boom on us with that jive. No, because we were celebrities. They never tell us what to do and what not to do. We go where we want to go. We played Ciro's in Hollywood, the biggest cafe, Ciro's in Hollywood. So I recall on opening night at Ciro's. You heard of the famous Ciro's? That was the cabaret. They never had no colored band, we were the first one. We played out there on a month's engagement, so I recall opening night, that's where all the Hollywood stars hung out.

So we was playing and the stage door let out from the stage in the alley. Got to come there, come to the stage door, to come to the stage so the first night, man, we ain't never run in no segregation, so the first night different people from New York -- New York actors and big stars, so they come over and so Duke went down and sit at the table with them because he's a star, so this cat, this Greek or whoever he was, he say listen Mr. Ellington, we don't allow the help to socialize with the guests, I say, 'Duke don't say nothing.' I don't hear him say

nothing, so the next night George Raft was big then, star, big party 16, ringside. They come in and he was a pal of mine, him and I like this, even today, he say, 'Sonny, when you get off come on down --'
(Recording interruption.)
So anyway, --
He said he wanted you to give him the news from New York.

Yeah, you know the gossip. Because before he went to Hollywood, the syndicate, he drove for my boss, chauffered for my boss. They sponsored his trip out there and he made good, so anyway, I was always -- I said 'I'll be right down, as soon as I'm off.' You and Duke come on down there.

So his favorite number was 'Sweet Georgia Brown'. We tore it up for him. Then my guy, New York cats, they let everybody know they was from New York. When you're a New Yorker, you let everybody know it. That's it.

So, all right, we finished, we go down, me and Duke. Here come the maitre-d. 'I'm sorry, Mr. Ellington, but the help don't sit at the table with the guests.' What that cat say that for? George Raft had 16 people, 'These are my friends, they can't sit down.' He said 'I tell you what you do,' he says let's take the whole table and put it in the alley there and sit everything up there, and we won't disturb your guests and Duke and Sonny going to have a nip,' they bought the whole table out in the

alley. We sit down and cabareted up a storm. That's right, and Georgie told this character, he said "Listen here, fellow, anytime I come in this place, and somebody's a personal friend of mine, don't you ever try to insult them, say, because I'll see that nobody comes in here. You will have to wait on other waiters. Said don't you ever do that to my friends. Never!"

He took a whole big table and sit it in the alley. The women were drinking champagne, there was some scotch. And I was telling them about New York. New York is jumping. He said, don't say no more, I got to get back there. But he was a rising star there, he couldn't -- one time he was making this Spanish picture. You know, he was a hell of a dancer, too. Man, I was on the set. My feet was killing me and he was doing a Spanish thing, had them soft Spanish slippers, so I went over to his dressing room. I said, "man, I can't make it. I got to have something soft to wear." So he give me a pair of Spanish slippers, put these one, and I was patting and drumming, felt like a million dollars.

He says, 'man, can you imagine I get all this money for hugging these people. Sonny, did you ever think it would end up like this?' He was a big star and him and Jimmy Durante, and all them. They're our friends, we worked together.
Jimmy Durante was in the show with us in Ziegfeld. See, those guys, those big stars, they're so easy, so congenial to get along with. And they raise up if somebody try to lay
a hype on you. They'll raise up. Even today. They'll do it. They are so nice. We were handled so nice, man.
And of course we lived up to all the publicity we had. We lived up and some more. We came first class. We played first class. We conducted ourselves first class, so we had it made.
Now, how did you -- when you all went into the Cotton Club, what was the personnel of the band? when you all first started there?
It was you -- When we started at the Cotton Club?
Yes.
No, We only had six pieces. We had to run it from six to eleven. I don't recall.
It was you, was Freddie Guy with the band?
Freddie.
Ellington, that's three. Bubber Miley. Tricky Sam, that's five.
Then we got Carney.
Harry Carney came with you. Bigard, and --
Bigard and Johnny.
Hodges, okay.
Lawrence Brown. Tizol.
Braud And on bass. Right. That was
the band you took into the Cotton Club with you.
Now, when did Irving Mills begin to manage the band?
He managed us at the Kentucky Club.
When you were at the Kentucky Club.

At the Kentucky Club. He become our official manager when in fact, he managed us when we went from the Kentucky Club too, to Cotton Club. He handled a lot of recordings for Duke's songs, because he never managed no band. But he had a big publishing house at 49th and Broadway in the Brill Building. He used to come here us all the time and he got those ideas and he -- that's when he said I am going to take you all and manage you. He didn't have no band. Later on he had Ina Ray Hutton's band, that's all.
Because he was the tops.
What kind of a guy was he?

Irving Mills. He was blue white diamond. He was the guy. He was the guy. He traveled with us. Everything first class, everytime you look around, he said 'I better get you guys another set of uniforms'. Everytime we opened up, he had boutonnaire flowers. He was there to see everything is perfect. In fact, I told you before, every show we had a different uniform from top to bottom.
When you all were there -- I was just reading a book by Rex Stewart* in which he said that because he-- when you guys were first working in the Cotton Club that the

guys, a lot of the guys in Harlem, because it was a segregated club, they didn't think a lot of the band, but different members of the band starting coming out and playing at different places like the Rhythm Club and others.

That was just a hangout. The Rhythm Club was where the guys, like I told you, they'd have different jam sessions and it was a place to hang out after you would get through work, a lot of guys would come in there and sit down and jam.

That's why they called it the Rhythm Club, went down there to play cards, or play pool, they had nice food, that's the Rhythm Club, it wasn't a regular cabaret or nothing like that. It was just like a social club for the musicians. It got so popular. But the guys would go down and if they feel like playing, they'd play. Wasn't no obligation. If the guy feel like he wanted to play something, you know, sit in and jam, go ahead and jam. Everybody went.
Did you go down there and jam much?

Me. After I got through work, I didn't jam nothing. I didn't put no jam on bread. I didn't jam nothing. What you talking about. If they'd pay me, I was for the almighty, a guy ask come on play something, you want to play something. I'd say no, I'll play some pool. I don't want to play no jam. It's all right. I never really went in for that jamming. I was playing for the almighty. Jam what.

But a lot of our guys would go down and play. Johnny would go down and play. Toby, all the guys. If they felt like playing, they'd play. Hawk used to go down and all the top. Jabo and all the guys would go down there and play.
Jabbo Smith played with the band for awhile, didn't he?
With us. No, he never played with us. No. He was a good friend of ours, but he never played with us.
Never played with the band. Didyou-- how did the band members feel about the segregated policy at the Cotton Club.

We were so busy -- we didn't pay it no mind. Because in the first place, we had colored people come up there, but the prices were so high. The average colored person back off. They could go to Small's Paradise and them clubs, and that -- when you come in the Cotton Club, you sit down, you're going to spend a lot of money. They didn't care if they were colored. You could come in. But the average guy, a rumor hear about this and that and the other, they'd back off. Cost a lot of money. Of course, them colored guys in the rackets, they associated like working for the guys, they'd come up and sit down and spend money and have a ball.
Yeah, that was what Jimmy Crawford who came in there told me. Told me the only colored people he knew were the racketeers.
That's right.
And Bill Robinson.

They never stopped Bill Robinson, he was a big star. They put the red carpet out for him. But the porter it was too much pressure, ordinary layman out there/ carrying them bricks and working, / he couldn't stand that. It was a regular Broadway production we put on, they could afford that. Stars, from the Ziegfeld show, and madames, all the big madames come up there.
How was the -- how did it come about that you all decided to go to Europe.
Oh, that's a good question. You know, Sophie Tucker, You heard of Sophie?
Yeah.

She was big, so one night she come up there with Lady Mountbatten, Lord Louis Mountbatten was a big man, an Englishman, he was Lord Louis Mountbatten. During the war he was in charge of a whole fleet, so he was a big man, one of the biggest and she was a cousin of the Queen, Lady Mountbatten was.

So Sophie, she was visiting in the United States and she was a friend of Sophie Tucker, because Sophie had played in Europe, and Sophie had brought her up because when you come to New York, if you didn't go to the Cotton Club, you hadn't seen New York, so she brought her to the Cotton Club.
We didn't know nothing about no Lord or Lady

Mountbatten so Sophie Tucker came over as soon as she come in, they introduced her, Miss Tucker's in the house. We played "Some of These Days." That was her big number then, written by this colored cat. I forget his name -- Shelton -- Shelton Thomas, he wrote that tune, and gave it to her and it made her famous, because she always mentioned it.

So we played her theme song, and then we went through our repertoire playing different numbers, so during the intermission she come backstage and go Duke, said Duke, I want you to meet some friends of mine so we could socialize all over the place, so Duke went out and met her and so she said, "Oh, I never heard no band like that. What do you call it the Cotton Club orchestra?" We did, you know, she said, "Oh, no, she said, if it were left to me I would call it the Aristocrats of Jazz." That's how we changed our name. Duke Ellington and the Aristocrats of Jazz.

So she said, "How would you like to come to London?" So Duke told her you could play all over Europe but no American bands played in London. You remember that, no American bands were allowed to play in London, so Duke said -- he still don't know who she is, so later on, that's Lady Mountbatten -- so she said, "Would you come to London? I would like for you to come to London. My people could hear you." So Duke said, "Oh, that would be fine."
Now, this was in 1933, about April or something like
that. She said, I'll fix it for you, so sure enough she did, and she come back up there about a couple weeks later and said it's all finished, it's all arranged, so that's how we come to London.
Wasn't no American band was allowed you could play in Paris, France and all over, but London, I don't know what -- one of them dumb ideas, no Americans, could play in London. You could play in Paris.
So we went there in July and we opened at the on July 5 Palladium/in 1931 --

'33. They had all the advertisement on the buses, the big two-story buses, advertised like a circus. At that time they had a band in London named Jack Hilton. He was like the Paul Whiteman that was here, so this cat he had a band, we had a couple of days before we opened in London, so I was riding somewhere and I heard this band playing and I said 'That sounds like our band.'

And the only reason I could tell the difference, it wasn't out band, when it come to individual solos, you know, it wasn't there. I said, What band is that? The guy said, 'That's Jack Hilton. The Jack Hilton.' He could imitate, had everything, note for note down, but the solos couldn't get them, because them guys played solo, how they felt. Played solo, how they felt, they played solo same number one time and another time

different, ad lib, like I used to tell Duke. Duke never wrote down them solos for Johnny and them, just write the skeleton and a gap and a couple choruses or something like that. But them ofays didn't have that.

We opened up at the Palladium, I'll never forget it. We did, they call it first and second house, and that's like a matinee in the afternoon. It's really the afternoon about three or four o'clock so we closed the first half of the program.

Now, we opened the first half -- the second half, all the others was English acts, so this big lady, she's a big star and I forget her name, big, big star, singer, she was in the middle of a song doing her act, so we were backstage-chasing -- in the dressing room, all you had to do was ring the bell and the waiter would come back and serve you, anything you wanted. That's the first time I ever saw that.

Them European acts were terrible. They was dead. They would tear you up. So the guys were nervous, you know, the guys walking up and down, you know, nervous, I say, 'Man, this is just another gig,' don't -- so Duke said, 'Press the button and bring all the boys a drink.' All of them had -- 'make them doubles.' So now this woman out here singing, and in the middle of the act, in the middle of the woman's song, right in the -- dead in the middle, the goddamn pit band goes into the National Anthem 'God Save the King,' or something, and every son of a bitch stood up. Them people around the curtain, I said, what happened, man, in walked the Prince of Wales. Now, I say, 'Man,' I never heard
no shit like this, this don't make no sense." He wasn't no bigger than this.
: About five feet tall?

Yeah, so after he sit down, she resumed her act. Now, at about 15 minutes intermission before the second part of the show come on, us, they opened the show with us. Now, we had been back there tasting, and everybody feeling fine, fine. No pain. Like I told you, we had our own stage, own stage rolled down and rolled back, had our own lights, the pinpoint lights, so Duke say, I want the stage completely dark, one pinpoint spot on Sonny because we opened with "Ring Dem Bells" and the stage is dark, the only thing you see -- the first thing you see is me, all them drums and chimes, da, da ------ man, I was --

The curtain broke, and the spot's on me and all you can is my face and my hands, hitting anything. I don't know whether it was right or wrong. Just making some noise. Man, about the eighth bar, they stood up, standing ovation. They hadn't seen the whole band yet. Stood up, cheers.

Cheers, youhear me? No exaggeration. I'm telling you like it was. Cheers. They got through the first number, then come Bailey and Derby, the dancers, two dancers, So, man, them cats could lay some wood, they could dance. So they come out and done their act and broke it up. So they act -- and me, I had never done that before, everytime they come out, I threw

arpeggio on the tympani, pedal--on tympani you know. That's what they call milking. I scared them half to death, so when they come off and we done that, everyone -- Ivie come up, naturally we killed them, and we closed our act with "Mood Indigo". Tricky and Barney and Lawrence -- no, Tricky -- who was it -- it was Tricky and Lawrence Brown and Carney come down and played just plain sweet melody and I was singing with the band then. And I was singing a high obbligato in back of it. It was faint, haunting, you know, that's how we closed.
Boy, I'm telling you -- it's on the writeup there. Did you ever see the writeup?
No. : Go ahead, we'll look at it after you show us.

So anyway when I come off, we had in my dressing room, Derby and Bailey, a whole big quart of booze. Say, "Man, keep that in, that bow, that was a highlight for us, keep that in." I said, "Man,...". They said, "No, you got to keep that in," so I kept it in all the way. Surefire, they're still bowing.

You know, it was so unexpected to see how things come to you. I had no idea of doing that, but just out of the (Unintelligible) on my left, I got mallets clear, just experimenting and I just on the/ and did arpeggio, and did the arpeggio on the pedal, I had no idea of doing that with them, but like something you feel like you're doing, you do it, and I did and they loved it.
Now, how long wereyou in England.

We stayed -- oh, we played the Palladium, we played a concert at the Elephant Castle, a big concert hall, we played another concert in Margate, England, and then we played Liverpool, played Blackpool and we played Birmingham, oh, about a month and a half, all over England.
About six weeks.
Yeah, then we left there and we went to Scotland. We went to Germany, we went to Sweden, Switzerland, Norway, Oslo, Norway, we went to Copenhagen, Denmark, Brussels, Belgium. We toured the continent.
All that was in....
Paris, 1933, Paris. We did the concerts in Paris, Paris Challeux, the big concert hall. That's right.
Did you see any difference between European audiences and American audiences?

Yeah. They were -- it's hard to say, but they were more enthusiastic for the simple reason -- it wasn't like in America, like you can go hear anybody you want. It was a rarity, and they were so overjoyed to see us in person and hear them in person that they were more enthusiastic.
Did the European women chase after musicians as much as they do in America?
Chase after what?
Did the women over there chase
after musicians as much as they chase after musicians in America.
What do you mean chase?
I mean, a lot of times musicians if they're popular, they're very popular with the women.
Well, at that time, we were always invited -- they were always giving up something for us, because when they like you, that was their way of showing their appreciation. Was over-enthusiastic.

I recall one time in Sweden on Duke's birthday, we were playing up there and 300 little girls, young teenagers they sang "Happy Birthday" in Swedish and walked down with flowers, and it happened to be on his birthday we were playing a concert, and during intermission they and another band played "Happy Birthday" and they all sang it in Swedish and all of them had a bouquet of flowers, right to the stage. You can imagine 300 bouquets of flowers and everybody singing, "Happy Birthday," yeah.
So you all were very well known in Europe, even before you got there, then?

We were the biggest thing since Barnum & Bailey. I tell you, they had on -- they call them buses here, they call them trams here, all on the side, like you see the bus, advertising on the side. The buses in New York, that's how it was.
How was it like in northern Europe, like when you went up to Norway and Denmark?
The same way, all over, everywhere. The same way. That's right. The same way.
You didn't have like any problems with accommodations or stuff you had here?

We stayed in the biggest hotels, we stayed in the biggest hotels, baby. I'm tell you like it is. We stayed in the biggest hotels. Every hotel we stayed in, because Irving Mills had our accommodations in front in the biggest hotels in every country. They fly -- like they fly for the dignitary the American flag was flown, on the hotel. We stayed there in honor of us. We stayed at the hotel -- just like they fly a -- a diplomat come and stay in a hotel, they fly his country's flag in the hotel, they flew the American flag for us.

I hear the cats talking about, we -- I say this, because I'm the only one in a position to speak now, because I'm one of the few-- I'm the only living original member of the band. We carried the flag, the American flag and the prestige for my people. I hear all these loudmouths talking about so and so, the black this, but we carried the flag for the American Negro all over the United States, 1933, '34 -- most of them loudmouths weren't born even now. We carried the flag, everywhere. I don't go for this colored jive. I am an

American Negro. You hear the cats say, the black this, I'm an American Negro, pal. We carried the flag and the dignity of the American, of my country all over the world. We were treated with the utmost respect. That's right. I can say -- I am proud to be a part of it, and my word, when a question come up, nobody tells me nothing. I say I was there, when you can say I was there, that eliminates all questions.

I was there, I didn't read that. I was there, baby. God is my judge, I was there. That's all I said. I was there, baby. People ask me different things, but I was there. I was a part of that. I made millions of people -- I was part of an organization that made millions of people happy.

Duke Ellington was a legend. He carried the dignity and the prestige of the colored race all over the world, respected, the dignity, so nobody -- he lived a few days, but he lived to see the more, he was a legend before he died. I'm living, I'm a living legend. That's no exaggeration.
Millions of people are my friends. I know. That's all I can say. I was there, baby. When you can say you was there, that's high-low jack and the game. You better believe it.

But let me tell you a little incident. This will kill you. So while I was in London in 1933, so Lord Beaverbrook, he's a Canadian, but he owns all the newspapers. You may have heard of him. He's big, big there. He would throw him a party so he throws this party at his mansion, you know, and
he had the guy that's married to the Queen now. He was just another turkey then, he wasn't married to her then. He hit the jackpot there.

So we don't have to carry no -- the guys carried their horns and didn't have to carry no bass and I didn't have to carry no drums. We play this party, Jack Hilton played till we got there. So we go in this party, we come in this party -- this is God's honest truth, this is not no illusion. This is the real thing. We come in this party and the place is crowded. At that time Jeannette McDonald, she was a big star, you know, she sang --
: She and Nelson Eddy.

She was there as a guest. Anna Mae Wong, remember her, some movie star and a gang of American movie stars, so we pop in there. I will never forget it. We were all dressed in white because it was in the summer, you know, in July, we had on white uniforms and special made, white special made shoes, all sharp, so this guy that's married to the Queen now, he grabbed Duke right away and sit him down at the piano stool and they start playing -- see, he play piano and start playing and Duke, wait a minute -- he say, 'I got 500 of your records.'
He padlocked Duke right away. I go over to the drums and a little cat's sitting down on the floor and so then we played, played and played and before we started playing there

is this big magnum of champagne in front of everybody and a bottle of Scotch -- bottle of brandy. One sitting there by me. I look at this fellow, I said, little taste, everything fine so now this cat sitting down on the floor he had one of them brandy snifters, big things, he's going with it. I still don't know who he is. So that goes on, so I say, 'Man, why do you...' (unintelligible)
So anyway, now me and him are buddies. He heard the guys, hey, Sonny -- Duke would say hey, Sonny, play so and so. We're going to play so and so.

So right away he pick up on my name, Sonny, so after awhile, he say, 'I can play the drum.' I say 'Yeah, come on man,' me and him tight now. We're juicing together. 'Go on and play, go ahead.' He say, 'I play the Charleston.' Play, ba, bab, you know, playing. I say 'Yeah, man, that's great.' So then (singing) I showed him how to play it fancy, and he said, 'Man, that's fine, can you show me that.' I say 'anytime,' still guzzling.

Now the people, the women start drifting by and they see this cat drifting by and I see all these women bow to this son of a bitch, curtsy you know, I say this cat must be -- and so the guy -- the waiter come up and say, 'Your Highness, some people want to see you.' You know who he was, the Prince of Wales. I never called him His Highness, he called me Sonny and I'd say, yeah, man, I am talking just like I'm talking to you.
I said, 'oh, you're the Prince of Wales.' He's heir to the throne.

So Wally Simpson from Baltimore, he finally married her, she hated my guts, hated Duke's guts. We were taking up too much attention, so he say, 'I'm leaving now. I got to go say hello to some friends, Sonny, I'll be right back though, don't you go nowhere.' 'I ain't going nowhere, Wale.' Call him the Wale, you know, he's the Prince of Wales, but that's too long, I say Wale, 'I'll be right here Wale when you get back.' He thought that was the cutest thing in the world.

He never forgot it. I called him the Wale. He followed us to Paris, to Scotland. He says, 'Sonny, what's my nickname?' I say 'You're the Wale, man, you're something else.' He thought that the was the greatest thing in the world. He never forgot it. Because we was friends up in Scotland, played a theatre, Sir Harry Lauder was the biggest Scotchman. We met him when he come in the Cotton Club, playing the Wintergarden in New York. He was the biggest thing that ever come out of Scotland. 'You take the high road, and I'll take the low road.' Them kind of people, man.
I look back, man, lady luck rode my shoulder a long time, baby.
How was Germany when you played up there the first time.
it was something else. Oh, man, I saw the Second World War jump off. We were there when the second World War jump off. The later years, you know. We went back to play a European

tour for a fellow named Baron Rudascor (phonetic) he was a nobleman from Sweden. We played on tour, played Germany, so we left Belgium and we went to Hamburg, Germany. We got in there at 11 o'clock in the morning. We supposed to take a pullman from there to Sweden, to Stockholm, so we were in this big station like Grand Central Station, in Hamburg, you know, and all we seen soldiers, uniforms, soldiers. We were about the only civilians in there, but they treat us nice.
We went up to the diner and an old Jewish couple went up there and they shoved them like dogs, didn't let them go nowhere. So we were standing up there.
Was this the first time -- was this 1933 or '39?

'39. It was '39, 1939. Hitler was in power then, so anyway we were standing in the station and all them German soldiers, everywhere you saw was uniforms. Youknow, they took our pullmans, the man had paid for them -- we stayed in that station from 11 o'clock in the morning until 12 o'clock at night, because they took all the transportation for the soldiers. They were moving then. That's right.

So one day we were standing up in the station and them guys in the German Air Corps, they call them Luftwaffe, they were the sharpest cats you ever saw. Them cats were so sharp, them uniforms, they was sharp, daddy. Young cats. I was standing there with Johnny Hodges and Toby and I had a little bottle
in my pocket. The whiskey was so bad, ain't nothing make it taste right, but I would drink it like water. So the cats, flyers there were four young German/, they come -- cut that off ---
(Recording interruption)
: After you told off the German guys of the Air Corps, you told them off in German and you showed them the gun.

Well, anyway, we got out of there and went to Sweden. We had the -- Irving Mills bribed some guys so he had a boat, he took us by boat over there. The guy that took all that transportation and everything, so now we stayed in Sweden for a while, and we had to go to some little town. I don't recall what it was -- I don't recall now, but we had to go over German borders, you know, and you had a set-up -- German thing. So now we're coming through the line and we had to show the passports.

We showed our passports and so now I'm in the line in back of Ivie, so I come to the line and they say, my passport said William Greer, that's my name. Sonny's a nickname, so the guy -- here's the guy with a major's uniform, one of the German officers, so when I get up to the line, he says, "Hello, Sonny, man, what do you know, how you doing". I said, "My name's William." Oh, he say, "Man, go ahead, your name's Sonny." I say, he said, "I saw you in Chicago, at Oriental Theatre."
: He saw you at the Oriental.

Yeah, wait, now get this. Now, he's a major in the German army. He took me aside, he said, 'I saw talking you at the Oriental Theatre,' soft, didn't want them other cats to hear him. I say, 'Yeah, What did we play?' He said, man do you still play 'Ring Dem Bells', and sing 'Mood Indigo'. He named every number we played.

So I look at this cat to be a big major in the German army, sharp, big cat. Oh, he was big. I said to him, I say, 'Man, if you know so much, what you doing in that uniform?' He look all around and he say, 'don't say nothing. He say I tell you when I see you in Chicago.' 'When will you be in Chicago?' I told him about three months from now. He say 'I'll come backstage and see you.'

I forgot all about it. So man, we're playing the Palace Theatre in Chicago, I come offstage and the doorman said, 'Hey, Sonny, there's a Colonel in the United States Army want to see you.' I say, 'Yeah, me.' Yeah. So I went down there and here's this cat. Now, he's a colonel in the -- I say, 'Man, what's going down, what's wrong with you.' He say, 'Well, man, I was in the Intelligence Department. What the hell, I told you I'd see you.'
Me and him went to the juice joint and had a ball.
How did you learn to speak German?
Oh, that's right, you learned to speak German in Long Branch. My teacher in high school. My teacher
had the orchestra.
That's right, you told me.
Had the orchestra, man. This cat was jiving -- I told the German teacher, I can beat him playing. Remember I toldyou that.
Bix Biederbecke was German, too.
I don't know. I guess so, German descent.
You said you were a good friend of his.

He lived in Davenport. His dad is a very dear friend of mine. He's buried at his home in Davenport, Iowa. Everytime we went to Davenport, we would go out and visit his people and go out to the cemetery and put some flowers on his grave.
Did you ever visit his family when he was alive?
No, I never met his people until after he died. Because he was in New York.
How did you meet Biederbecke?
Just hanging out. All of them come to Harlem. Every one of them came to Harlem see what they could learn. All of them came.
I remember you told me last time we talked that he was a good trumpet player, but he wasn't --

Oh, no, you couldn't put him up on the stage with Louis Armstrong with a derrick, man. None of them cats dumb enough to get up on the stage and saxophone players, back of Hawk and all them guys. Never happen. They drink, but they never drank that much.
No, they don't get that drunk. They would get scalded so fast it wasn't even funny.
Did you know Jimmy Harrison.
Trombone player?
Yeah.

Jimmy, good pal of mine. He play up there at the Savoy with Chick Webb. Yeah, he was something else. Jimmy Harrison, Big Jimmy. He big cat about as big as you. Jimmy's a little taller than you, I think. He -- Big Sid the drummer and Big Jimmy, he could play some trombone too. He's something else. I know them guys. We hung out.
He and Jack Teagarden used to hang out together.
Yeah, yeah. Poppa T. I played with him too.
What did you think of Teagarden?

Oh, fine, fine, yeah, he was something else. Poppa T was something else. He played fine, man. Strictly New Orleans Poppa T. I nicknamed him Poppa T. Miff Mole was another trombone player. He's good. He was a studio
man, he could play a trombone, and all of them idolized Lawrence though, when they heard Brown, the top come off, the cap come off.

Lawrence Brown, Lawrence was, out of all our guys, he was the most unassuming guy -- he didn't have them instincts like we had. We called him Sweetie. Ben Webster called him Sweetie. / Sweetie Brown. Yeah, man, Sweetie was something else. He was a heavy lover. He say, hey sweetie come on, man, he didn't drink nothing, didn't smoke, but he was -- with them women, he was all right. Poor Lawrence, nice guy, they all take advantage of him. A nice guy, get the/stick all the time.

Today is Friday and I am going to try to come see you Monday.
Good.
And probably like next Friday, we'll be finished.

Right. 2 o'clock.

I want to try and : -- get some background into the scene that you guys were on. Like Rex Stewart's book, Jazz Masters of the 1930's, he says that Baron Wilkins Club was one of the places you guys --
It was the club, yeah.
That was THE club?
