Baron Wilkins we had -- Ada Ward, Ada Brisktop got us the job there.
Oh, working at Baron Wilkins place?
Yeah, because she was hostess there. She got us this job in June and the business just tripled over night. The news spread and all the people from downtown started --

it got to be one of the clubs, they would come there, see. So all the musicians, our friends, they'd come in. But it was so small, we didn't have room to accommodate them guys, like six men playing. It couldn't do it. I mean, we -- he never turned them away but as far as playing, they come to listen. All of them come to listen, the white musicians, colored musicians.
What kind of a person was Baron Wilkins himself?

A very unassuming man, you know. Very quiet-spoken. But when he said something, he meant it. He was high with the syndicate, you know. And Baron Wilkins, he was stubborn. That's how he got killed, he was very stubborn. If he didn't think something was right he'd just go ahead and forgot it.
I was walking down 7th Avenue the day he got shot. By Yellow Charleston (PHONETIC), a guy named Yellow Charleston.
Yellow Charleston?
That was his name. After they got him and everything, because he didn't try and run away. It was one of those things, you know, from high up it got pinpointed because he was stubborn.
What did they want to do? Did they want to take over his place?
I don't know. I really don't know whether they wanted to take over. No, after he got shot the place
folded, you know. It was never no more like that. That was it.
You remember what year it happened?
No, that was in the twenties.
Was this before or after you all went in the Cotton Club?
That was before.
Before you went in, he got killed?
Before we ever went to the Cotton Club.
He was killed before then?

Yeah, just before then. That was our next gig, the Kentucky Club -- not the Cotton Club, the Kentucky Club down 49th and Broadway. Because I wasn't paying the Cotton Club no mind, man, we was making so much money down there.
(Laughter.)

The Cotton Club was a million miles away from us. It took me a long time to get acclimated to working in the Cotton Club. That thing broke my heart, man, much money as I was -- I was a little nephew. Them cats were looking out for me. Man, they had a blanket over top of me. I was making money right and left.
But you always got along with people pretty quickly.
Yeah, well, understand, I like people

and people like me. I don't know what it was, I don't know what it is, even to this day. But people and I always got along, all kinds of people. Because -- I don't know, just maybe they -- I'm a hell of a liar and a good actor.
(Laughter.)

They like that, you see. They like me, because if I thought someone was right I'd come on. I didn't know the word "back". Because a lot of the times I'd be coming -- standing on Broadway and 49th Street and across the street was Lindsey's (Lindy's) a very famous -- that was the hangout for all the big gangsters in New York, Lindsey's, right at 49th and Broadway. Those racketeers would be arguing about anything. So one of them would spot me and say, "come here, Sonny, so and so . . ." Now, I don't know how they bet, but I'd kind of see my man on the side, and I'd know he'd say... I'd say, "How you going today? All you got to say is "No." I'd say no, and make my point. And here'd come a little tip of something. Nice taste.

It was beautiful. And Connie, that owned Connie's, he was always arguing. Just a horserace or something, what the hell do I know about the horses. But he'd ask me; I'd just go with him. And he would collect the bets. Stood me $20.00 or something. That was a whole lot of money then. I sneaked downtown to stand out in front of Bill (Inaudible). I know they're going to start some arguing. They called me over,

across the street. And I was settling. Like one time Sherman Billingsley Billings at the 21 Club, Sherman Billings, you had to show your birth certificate to go in. I knew this guy when he had one of them jive drugstores. There wasn't no drugs in the place but in the back he was selling/whisky--- Before he got downtown and got high class.

So he was selling homemade gin for $1.00 a quart. There wasn't no fifths then. So I make my gin under (unintelligible) 75 cents. If you had a job, you could carry it. And he hated my guts. No kidding, he hated my guts. So I always took what I could. I laid mine down for 75 cents, you could (unintelligible) me. "Give me a bottle of that stuff." "Okay." If You had a gig or something, "Okay, baby, I see it. Go on." I'd make it and sell it.
Oh, you made gin, too, did you?

I made everything. I made some soda, anything. I tell you, man, I was up on -- I studied, man. I studied. I think, because New York was a jungle, you've got to realize first off, New York was a jungle. So you had to look at all angles, you know. And I looked at it, I studied. I saw cats doing something over there, I'd know nothing about it; I'm going to watch them real close and pick up on it. So I was there.
I got to survive. I had to survive. I ain't playing them drums no mind. I got to survive. So I made my little
gin and sell it. If you had a job, you could carry it. You'd all write your name, perfect, and I'd lay it on you. I did all right, too. You better believe I done all right, man.

I know a lot of -- that life is -- I have fond memories. They are real fond memories. And I look back at the things happening, those kinds of days. It makes me feel proud, I could match up to what was happening. I'm not proud -- I never harmed nobody but myself in my life. And I love people, because without people you and me and nobody else is nothing. If you're dealing with the public, you have to have a certain amount of affection for people to survive. I love everybody. You've seen me in action, I love people, people love me.
Well, tell me this, when you were -- were you the one in the band that had the most kind of like know-how in terms of how -- the corners to get around?

Yeah, I was the one. You know, it was a brand new whole world for Duke and the boys, it was a brand new world. They didn't know that stuff. But I was always involved in it from time beginning. I was involved in night life. I recorded. I was there. So I just picked up fast on all that stuff. And, you know, it was always looking for a curve, man I was looking for a curve.
You see, me and Fats and all the guys, and all of us, we were -- Willie 'the Lion' --, we were always looking for a curve, what we call a curve. We didn't miss nothing.
We didn't miss nothing. We were looking for the curve and we worked for each other. We were a closely knit bunch of guys.
Those were your closest friends, Will the Lion Smith and --

Oh, I mean professionals, Will the Lion, Corky, Lippy, all piano players. James P. and all them guys. I hung with them. I had a great affection for them guys. Not only as to how they could play, but as persons. We hung out together because if one of them got a gig, they would cut me in. If I heard of something, I would tip them to it and they would catch on.

Oh, we had New York parlor socials locked up. There wasn't no parlor social if one of us was there and then naturally they had me there, too. Wasn't making but a dollar a night. Give me a dollar, all the food, all the drinks you want-- survival.
Now, these parlor socials, what kind of people would give them?
They call them people -- they had a name for them, they call them Dicties (PHONETIC), they live up on Sugar Hill.
Like Jame] Terrace and Edgecombe?
Way -- oh, way up there, right. They'd give a parlor social every Saturday. That goes towards the

room rent. Or something, you know. Ain't no musicians to play unless Big Fatso, Willie the Lion. We played, you know. $1.00. $1.00 a night, all the food, all you could drink. You want to take some home, beautiful. And everybody comes. They pass out invitations like they pass out handbills. That was real parlor socials. Ain't no bands played there, just pianos. That's it.
Now, what did you do when you went there?
Just played drums.
Oh, it was piano and drums?
Piano and drums.
Did you sing at any of them?

No, this was my voice. Ain't no songs because they wasn't paying that kind of money for $1.00. I always put my voice in -- no songs for $1.00. I'd just play along and talk a lot, up off the wall, with lot of people, you know. Cause everybody was talking off the wall, everybody scheming. And I'm right in the middle of it.

And I'd take a hat. I'd say, "I think I'll take this home, with me." Get some chicken, potato salad, go home and carry me three days. That's how we saved, carry me three days. Put it in a little drawer in the living room, close the drawer. If the doorbell rings, "who is it?" I'd close the drawer, open the door. I kept all that chicken and turkey and ham in a drawer. Cat comes in I didn't invite, I ain't
never going to pull out the drawer. That was it. We lived that way. That was it, man.
This is the way you made it when you first got to New York?

Yeah. That was it, babe. We called it cold kina (PHONETIC), that was the name of it, cold kina. Cold food, they called it cold kina. I had a drawer full of turkey and ham and potato salad. Never opened the drawer if there was some strangers there or somebody come that wasn't a close friend of mine. Ain't going to never pull that drawer out.
Did you ever meet -- there was a rich guy up in Harlem during those years who was kidnapped at one time, Casper Holstein (PHONETIC).

Casper Hostein, I know him, the number man. Yeah, he was one of the few colored guys -- he was a numbers back-up. They kidnapped him, sure. But they turned him loose because he was closely associated. 'Cause they put the word out, "turn him loose." Whenever the Syndicate says, "that's my man," that was it. That was it.
Now, when you first came to New York, who controlled the numbers?
Dutch Schultz.
Dutch Schultz controlled the numbers?
Yeah, Dutch Schultz.
Did you know him?

I've seen him. But my man was the top man. My man was a top man. He was over Dutch Schultz, Al Capone and all of them. He wasn't a -- a little, tiny guy. Talked like a girl. Never raised his voice. Owney Madden. Owney Madden. He owned the Cotton Club. When he said something, that was it. And he loved -- he loved Duke because him and Duke used to sit up and play "Grits" and all that, "Coon Can" all night long after the club closed. Me, I'm ready to run. When the last note hit, I'm gone. I say, I don't play that game, I don't know anything about them games.

But he loved Duke and he loved me. And his influence was so powerful that we was always in the clear. He'd say, "Duke and Sonny are my boys." Guys, even I recall one time, first time we ever played the theater in Chicago, you know, I told you about that. So we come off the stage after the first show. I came off the stage, I'm the last one off the stage because the other guys just sat down. Taft But I was the last one because I had all the equipment, I had to check to see all that. I'd come off and I wanted to see Duke about something, I don't know, I don't know whether it was money or anything, they all Irving Mills, in Duke's office.
So I come off and standing up in Duke's dressing room was two big cats. I come off, I'm going in the room. I don't know who they are. And one guy, he stopped me. He said,

You can't go in there. I said, 'I got to go in there and see see about this show.' 'You can't go in now, Mr. -- what the hell was his name. Later he was going to be -- became the head of the musician's union. Petrillo, you heard of Petrillo?
Yeah, Petrillo.

"Mr. Petrillo's in there. You can't go in." I say, "Man, I'm talking about the show. I've got to go in." So I brushed past them and went in. So this cat, Petrillo, was standing up there, man, and these guys were his bodyguards. He was standing up there, talking to Duke, pointing his finger. "You can't do this, you can't do that."

So I say to Duke, "What's the matter, man?" He say, "This guy's trying to give me a hard time." Now, they still don't know Owney Madden (PHONETIC) is our representative -- boss. I say, "Get on the phone, call this number." We had to get a private number. They call this number. So Petrillo say, "Who you calling?" I say, "The man who owns our band." And he knew -- he knew the number, you know.

So man, he turn around and look at me. "Don't call it." I say, "Oh, yeah, let me call him up." "No." "Yeah, I'd rather call this." I say, "You all are interfering with my living. I've got to call this." So our road manager had a little Jewish road manager, Sam Flashnick (PHONETIC). He called the number. So Owney answered; said, "Put him on." What he said
I never know but when he got through talking to this cat, this cat was this small.
He just melted down, huh?

Melted. They was shaking down all the acts that had come through. And he told them, "Listen, as long as my band's in Chicago, see all courtesies are extended. And don't you ever come around and try to give them a hard time. That's what they told him.

Now, you see a snake, I know a snake. I'll tell you a definition of it. A snake is a guy when he find out that he's beneath you, he wants to put his arms around you and be your buddy. I said, "Oh, no." He said, "My daughter's having a party. Can some of the band play, about four or five of the guys come over to play a little music for her?" I said, "Look, I told Petrillo, fellow, I wouldn't play at your funeral if you paid me." Uh-uh, ain't no days like that.

But he had Earl Hines and all them guys cowered. I said, "You got the wrong people." And he cooled way down and he never forgot it. And I meant it. And them big guys said, "I didn't know you knew him." I said, "Yeah, he's my boss." I said, "When you don't know something, ask somebody something. Because a whole lot of people smarter than you, baby." I said, "I been in more cities than you been in toilets. Don't lay that down on me."
So there was a little guy called "Machine". Machine McGirk.
Machinegun McGirt?

Machinegun McGirt. A little sharp cat. Sharp, about my size, who come down to the theater. He say, "Duke, I had a call, I'm supposed to look out for you guys." And right away he attaches himself to me. I said, "Man, I don't need nobody." And I used to keep this cat out until all hours of the night. And he loved it. It got so we loved each other. Where ever you'd see me, he'd be right there somewhere. He was sharp. And all of them knew him, you know. Years ago at this cafe.
Where's this cafe in Chicago? Mike DeLisa and his brother had a cafe.
Oh, the Club DeLisa?

Club DeLisa. And George Kirby was a busboy there. That's where I first heard him. Me and Machine we closed it every night. I'd walk out there at 6:00 o'clock now and go on stage at 11:00. I'm scared to go home so I'd go to the theater and lay down on my cot. My valet (table) would bring me a pint of whisky and coffee. I made eight hours sleep. Man, I'd get up there and drill that band. The cats was betting in Chicago, Sonny will never make it. And I was the best one on the stage. Duke was yawning, he's tired. Ben, all of them tired and I was shouting it up. I'd raise the tempo a little bit and shout them cats, man, down! When they get offstage, I'm ready to faint. I can go upstairs and fall
out. Them were good days, man.
Was that the way when you -- when the band was a little bit tired you'd spark the tempo up just a little bit?

Just a trifle. Just enough to make it exciting. Anything, I didn't care what it was, I'd pick it up just a notch and keep them guys alert through the first show then they could relax you know. And the guys would all curse me out, man. "Man, why you do that?" I'd say, "Well, I go home early and go to sleep." I ain't saw no bed.
(Laughter.)
Duke was looking at me. Man, I think that's how he started playing the piano with his back to the audience. You saw Duke?
Yeah.

Was his back to the audience? He would be playing the piano and yawning. And I would whistle down, "Wake up, you so and so. Man, come on, let's take it." But I love him. That was my guy, baby. And the whole band was my guys.
My job, like I told you, was to keep the band on a level ke Because all bands, they would start low and accelerate, you know. But our band, with all them stars, smooth as velvet.
How did you -- do you have anything
you recall about Chicago you wanted to say before I interrupted you about the tempo?

Let me see. No. I recall, I recall one night they had Benny Goodman billed as the King of Swing. He had that big band and quartet. So there was a big affair at the Auditorium in Chicago. And we come over. You know, they were donating the entertainment for charity. So we went over for the theater group. Benny Goodman was on there, playing the Savoy" same thing he's playing now, "Stompin' at" and all that junk.

So Fats was in the audience. Right there he said, "Hey, Duke, you direct, I'm going to play with that band." So Fats played the piano. They put the thing -- where he stopped, that's where we started. We'd lay it on him. And we closed with "Dimenuendo -- "
And "Cresendo."

Laid it on this turkey and the roof fell in. He stopped speaking to Fats, he stopped speaking to Duke. We killed him. This turkey walking around with Fletcher arrangements. Because that's where he got stopped. He bought Fletcher's book and we killed him. Killed this turkey dead. When that six brass showed up and them cats at the end, a "Cresendo" and "Dimenuendo" and start howling, Barly bar the door, man. He was a dead duck, man. You'd better believe it. That's the only time he ever run against him because we knew it. We didn't do it intentioned. We just let him know what

what was happening. He got proud, walking around, Benny Goodman. As a clarinet player, Barney would kill him. And if Barney would kill him, Jimmy Hamilton would kill him. Kill him dead. There you go. Stampede him man. It was one of those things. That was Chicago.

I was so busy. Chicago was a toddling town but windy. Man, wasn't no joint that I ever missed. Beautiful, beautiful. Ray Nance was playing down in the basement, in a bar, with Jimmy Noone that played clarinet, them cats and a guitar and a bass, them cats could play, man. That's the first time I saw him. What's that song, what's Jimmy's theme song? We play it, me and Brooks play it all the time. Clarinet thing. Man, Chicago was THE town.
Not "High Society"?

No, not "High Society". That's New Orleans. (Humming.) Nice, pretty tune. He signed off and signed on with it. Can't think of that name. But anyway, he played that and I was just up there in heaven, them guys played so sweet. Played so beautifully, man.
Is that where you first heard Ray Nance?
Yeah, he was playing with them. We used to close this joint up every morning. And we'd go upstairs. upstairs to Struggle go to bed. But that was it. Man.
Did you have anything to do with
No, Duke heard him in person.
No, I mean did you --
No, I didn't influence Duke one way or the other.
No, but did you tell him about Ray Nance after you heard him?

Well, Duke usually came every night because he was downstairs in the cafe where we lived. Duke lived there, we all lived there. Duke would be having one of his dreams and he saw where Ray could fit in the band. Ray played trumpet and the violin, that was it. And sing. You know, Duke was on the lookout for everything. Duke gobbled him right up.
And the Captain -- I called him Captain. Beautiful guy.
Let me see, you had for a little while -- there was some guys in the band you didn't talk about last time.
Who's that?
Rudy Jackson was one.

Oh, he played saxophone. Rudy Jackson, Brother Rudy, yeah. Rudy Jackson. He just played -- Rudy Jackson played with us -- let me see, he played with us at Salem Willows. But Rudy played with the band before Carny.

He played nice. Not exciteable. He played the saxophone. But after Duke heard Carney, Carney come down with his clarinet in a paper bag. Young kid. And played, so Duke latched onto him. We had Carney and Rudy for a while so after we come back to New York he sent for Carney to come and join us. Carney was with us before Johnny Hodges. Johnny was playing with Nelson, the trumpet player.
There's another guy here, Nelson Kincaid.
Trumpet player? Yeah, he went with us -- let me see. He went with us to Europe, you know. Uh-huh. Nelson Kincaid, the trumpet player. And he stayed in Europe. I guess he's still there.
Here's Rudy Jackson -- no, not Rudy Jackson. No, that's what you call him. Rudy hasn't got a picture.
Now, tell me, after you guys -- you told me how Ivie Anderson joined the band. How did Johnny Hodges come into the band?

Johnny was playing with Chick Webb at the Savoy. And Bechat (PHONETIC) had left us and gone somewhere. So Duke got -- he heard about Johnny so he offered Johnny a job. Johnny was with Chick Webb and Cootie was with Chick Webb. So Duke liked Johnny Hodges and he offered him more money than he made with Chick, and a steady job. So he picked up with him.
Boy, I liked this book. This was when we got to Europe.
MR. : Derek Jewell's "Portrait of Duke Ellington".
Hell of a book.
MR. : So what kind of guy was Johnny Hodges?

Oh, Johnny was beautiful. My sidekick. MR. : Oh, he was fast like you, then? MR. GREER: Oh, me and Johnny was ham and eggs. Johnny was so good. No kidding. Soon as he opened his eyes, he'd call my room. "Hey, man, where we going?" My room or Toby, me and Johnny and Toby. Inseparable. Up until the time he died, where he went, I went. Where I went, he went. Toby the same way. Minute he opened his eyes, first thing he wants to find about Johnny and me. We were like that.

Of course, Duke was the general and we were the three hang-outs. That's right. He was a beautiful guy, that's all I can say. There was only one guy like Johnny because he was crazy like I am, crazy like Toby was. So like ham and eggs. He was beautiful.

Well, I tell you, we had a bunch of guys, I wouldn't say we were crazy. We had a bunch of guys that was like a family, you know. The Ellington organization was a family. Which was very unique, you don't catch a bunch of stars

together, 10 or 12 guys, that the harmony is so perfect. Because Duke was for his guys. Even when he died, right or wrong, Duke never deserted his boys. There was one word Duke never said to us in all the years we associated. He never said "no" if a crisis arised. He never said "no." He stood in back of his boys. They were his family.
Do you have any examples you recall, stand out in your mind?

No, not no one thing. The guys were always getting into mischief, you know. All they had to do was call the manager and Duke would tell him, "Go down and see what's happening." He was there. Night or day.

No, we never got in no serious mischief. Our marks with the public was clean-cut. Clean-cut, we never had no serious -- you know, like guys getting in trouble. We didn't have that. Because he would constantly preach to the guys, be careful, don't get in no hassles. And we never did. Because we were always together. They had cliques in the band, naturally, but we never got in no trouble.
What were some of the cliques in the band?

Well, I hung out with everybody. I was everybody's boy. But my closest friend in the band was Toby and Johnny. They were my closest friends. Now, Tricky and the trumpet player, Bubber and -- let me see who they hung
around with. They had a little clique.
Nanton hung out with Charlie Irvis for a while, didn't he?

Yeah. Well, trumpet players. Then Ray hung out with Tricky after Charlie Irvis left the band. He hung out with Tricky. Ray Nance was all over the scene, you know, he was a cocky kid, he was all over. But what I mean, we didn't hang out with certain guys. We'd just automatically get together and go somewhere. If we run into the guys, we would band together and go -- well, we always never forgot we were a family, you know. We were all for one and one for all.
So how were the rehearsals in the band? Did you all rehearse a lot?

Oh, yeah. Duke was very exact. He was exact. He would write his dreams. I always called them his dreams, you know. Like numbers he would write, he would write them down, rehearse a couple hours, three hours, a recording session we rehearsed a day, four or five hours and then record. So when we got in the studio, time was valuable. We didn't do a lot of stumbling. We rehearsed a lot. Like we had something important, like to play a concert or play a recording, he would have everything written out. We rehearsed it two or three times so when we first got to the studio, we'd bat it down once for balance and tape it. That's right.
Do you think that he -- I noticed that in listening to the recordings of Ellington's band, you all got a much better recording sound than a lot of other bands.

Yeah, we had a special guy, Bob, I don't know his last name. It wasn't like recording now. It had two notes, there wasn't no one guy off key. This guy -- Duke would stand off, when a guy over there was a little off, he would stop it and correct it. Not like now, all these bums that are playing "My mama and hey, baby, yagga dagga dagga." Because the worse you sound now, the more successful you are. But it wasn't like that. It had to be exact and perfect. Balance, tonation, everything. You get them guys, the Skyrise or Tramps or them funny names, them guys, and the broads singing "Baby, baby, my man done me wrong," it's ridiculous. They get a $3.00 guitar, hair long, sing, "the wind is blowing, the water's wet."
(Laughter.)

Right away, right away, these guys like Mike Douglas and them guys, they tote them up and the first thing, "How many gold records you got?" "I got a dozen". They must give them away like handbills because talent-wise, they're nothing. They don't even know when the song ends. You hear them everyday, How can you tell when the song ends, when they end a song. They don't know when to bow, they have no finesse,
nothing.

And them country singers are living jokes. They didn't know cats wore shoes until the Second World War come along. And they had the nerve to bar -- when we're shouting about race records, we couldn't even -- they didn't play our records down there in Nashville and the South.

I made some records with Ivory Joe Hunter, he used to be a piano player and singer. Blow them cats! Clarence Williams. They're nothing. They ain't even good imitators. Not meaning to knock -- well, I'm telling it like it is because I was there. The greatest thing I ever say to you and anybody else, doing an interview, talking to you, I just say one thing: I was there. That eliminates everything. I was there. I went through that. And there's no substitute for experience.
Well now, when you all were -- the band was -- you say it was a very exacting kind of band?

When we recorded, we had to do it exact. Our recorder, our chief recorder, demanded that was exact. All horns tuned and syncopation, everything was perfect. Unless -- they were discarded. It wasn't, "Let's get this done and get through." No, babe, it had to be perfect. That's why so many of our records were successful, you know what I mean?
Well, that was why the sound of the band came off a lot.
We had a man, his job was to see every-
thing was perfect. He wasn't just a recorder, he knew the recording business backwards. He saw everything was -- all instruments in tune, everything went down smooth, timing was perfect, that was it.
If a guy knew something was wrong, he'd stop it right away.
Well now, what were -- like when you all first started recording, though, you recorded under a lot of different names like the Harlem Footwarmers?

Anybody was paying the price -- how many men you want? Recorded under so many names it wasn't even funny. But it was the guys out of the band. Tack a name onto them and make the record. Sonny Greer and his Memphis Men. I recorded, took me five or six cats and make that bread, real fast. That's what you call a fast hustle. That's right. But we had five or six guys, seven or eight. Record with anybody, "You got a recording date? Need some men." And we were there.
But when it come down to nitty gritty, the Ellington organization, Duke's name was never on them. Because he's never played piano on them things. We had free reins to do anything we wanted.

Now, what bands do you think -- I wanted to ask you because I read once that Harry Carney said he remembered a battle of the bands in which Coleman Hawkins cut the whole Ellington band. Do you remember that?
No, never happened. Never happened. Hawk was at the top of the heap but he -- now, Hawk and I were, for many years -- when it was Mamie Smith.
Oh, with Mamie Smith and the Jazz Hounds?

Yeah. With a trumpet player, what was his name? He was a hell of a guy, Bubber had to cut him down to size. Johnny somebody. He'd play, he'd do a whole lot of -- Bubber ate him up. Bubber took his plunger and killed him. Hawk was in the band. That's the first time I saw Hawk, Lincoln(?) Theater, Mamie Smith, a very prominent singer.
Right. Blues singer.)

Yeah, she was something else. But Hawk play in that side band? No way. 'Cause Bechet and Bubber and (Tricky), Bechet would take that napkin I was telling you about and put it -- and wash him away. No way in the world he could survive that. I wouldn't kid. He was good but he wasn't that good. And he knew it. And wasn't enough money in New York to make him buck our band. No way! Because we had some hot guys too, on that tenor sax. We had some tough guys. Oh, Ben was laying back there. Ben was playing -- he was Ben's idol. Ben could duplicate him like ham and eggs.
He'd come up there with that jive, he may catch one of them little lightweights or something like that. Hawk could play. I have the utmost respect for -- he was beautiful,
could play. He had a wide range. He was like Johnny Hodges on his horn. He had a terrific brain and he could duplicate on his horn, like Johnny Hodges.

There was only one Johnny Hodges, there's only one Hawk. Hawk was the same way, same way as Johnny. And they were inseparable friends. Hawk was (inaudible)--the closest guy to Hawk was Don Byas. You heard Don Byas?
Oh, yeah.

We went to Europe and Duke hired Don Byas just as a guest soloist. He played -- what's that song -- "Oh, Danny Boy." In four different tempos. Kill you. Don Byas, he was my running mate. He'd say, man -- he lived in Europe. "Man, you --
(End of side A as recorded.)
He was fine. But he was -- he wasn't no bigger than me. Something else, he was something else, man. Yeah, Django Reinhardt --
Yeah, Django Reinhardt played in the band.

We brought him from Europe. First time ever in America, played at Carnegie Hall. The gypsy, from the French Hot Five. --man, that cat and guitars, make it talk. Nobody played like -- only had three fingers on one of his hands.
Yeah, his left hand.
Bov, but that cat, oh, God. He was something else.
What kind of a guy was he? Did he speak much English?

None. Little tiny. So I body-guarded him. I remember one time we played a concert in Pittsburgh. So he, a French boy living here, so he say, "Come on, Sonny, we go have a drink." I say, all right. So we go in this high class joint, we stand up at the bar, cat don't pay him no mind. So, you know, French hot, so he knock on the bar. "Service". And the guy says, "I can serve you, Mister," but he wouldn't serve me. "What'd he say that for?" Had to drag the guy out of the bar. He wanted to create a scene. I said, "Man, it's nothing. Forget it." He say, oh, a lot of French. I don't know what the hell he was saying but I know it was hot.

So the guy, after he found out who we were, he apologized. "Come in." So I say, "We don't want to come in your bar, Mister. You don't do me no favor, I spend the money. I owe you nothing. Forget it. You drink it." Anyway, he couldn't even give it to me. I'm hot now. So we go, go back down Wiley Avenue (unintelligible) Ball! Ball! Ball! But you're a you see, /the average thing the guys make, they make a mistake. They see a colored guy so right away they category them all as one. They don't give you any consideration that you have

more brains than they do. So ain't no cat, ain't ever born a cat could think he'd do me a favor when I'm spending my money. Uh-uh. Because I come in a gentleman, I treat this place with respect. So what am I? So I won't bother about it. Understand what I mean?
Yeah, of course.

I never in my life -- I look back sometimes, it gets frightening. I never in my life took water from nobody. Nobody, and I've been in some of the worst dives, it frightens me now, in the world. But I always stood up for my rights and dignity, anywhere, in Europe and America. All you got to say, you know, "Okay, I see you later." (Laughter.) Oh, I could write a book on some of the episodes in my life. It would be a best seller.
You probably should.

For laughs. Just for laughs. I don't mean, just giving incidents for laughs, man. But Duke nicknamed -- my nickname with Duke was "Nasty". He always called me Nasty. "Hey, Nasty?" I'd say, "Yeah, Man?" so and so and so. That was my nickname.

Duke called me Sonny lots of times but when he wanted something important, hey, Nasty. Even when he wrote the book, "Music is my Mistress", he used to call me 3:00, 4:00 o'clock in the morning to recall instances 20 years ago. I'd say, "Man, call me back later. I can't talk now." So he'd call
my wife, say, "Hey, Mil, wake him up." I'd say, Oh, God. But he understood. I would come up with names.

Like his first show, the Las Vegas time and New York time is different. He would call, I'd say, "Man, what you calling me this -- say, your time is different." I'd say, "Don't call me, Man." He would ask me, "What was that guy's name in Washington or New York, 20 years ago?" I'd say, "Call me tomorrow and I'll tell you." He'd call and I'd have it right on the nose. He knew I'd remember, you know.
Do you remember any other incidents that took place with you and Django Reinhardt? Not so much bad, but any kind. You know, when you all were running around together.
Playing wise or just running around together?
Both.

No. I remember we were playing a concert in -- when was it? Doing a concert, I think it was in Boston. At the Auditorium in Boston. So we were -- we had about an hour before -- we always got to the place an hour or so, the band would be relaxed. So me and him, he was sitting backstage playing one of the things he used to play with Hot Five, a fast thing, you know. So I had some brushes and a newspaper. So just me and him was playing. He said, "I like that." Duke come in and say, "I like that." So as a surprise encore, we
done it.
The duet?

Me and him and Duke was playing a little light background in the back. Us three. And Jimmy Blanton on bass. We done it, it was a big thing. Duke said, keep it. I don't know what's it called, he had some fancy name for it. But he used to play it with the French Hot Five. That was one thing.
What did you think -- go ahead, did you have something else you wanted to say?
No.
What did you think of Charlie Christian? Did you meet him?
Oh, I've heard with him many times. Charlie Christian -- guitar player?
Yes.
Beautiful. The end. The last word. Charlie Christian was a famous guitarist. Beautiful. They still talking about him. And he's been dead a long time.
Did you and him ever hang out together?

Uh-uh. We wasn't close because our paths didn't cross that much. But I knew him. Whenever he played we would go hear him. But we were what you call moving fast. And he was different things but accidentally we'd
cross each other and we'd sit and talk about New York, have some fun. But that's all.
What kind of a guy did he strike you as?
He strike me as a beautiful person. Very congenial, lovely. His success never went to his head, he was just a level guy. Everybody loved the cat. He was beautiful.
Did he ever talk about being in Goodman's band? Talk about being in Benny Goodman's band?

No, no, no. It was a high honor because at this time the Iron Curtain was up, you know. I give Benny Goodman credit. He was the first one to break through when he got Hamp and Teddy ___. He was the first one to present the colored musicians with his band. Because before then it wasn't heard of. Wasn't heard of. But a band with that reputation with colored musicians, it was a high honor. I give Benny very much credit. He kind of opened the door. It eased open a little bit, you know. Eased open a little bit because people that are prejudiced -- there's still a lot of it, don't let nobody kid you. There's still a lot of it now days.

New York was like New York, Georgia. I told you how they acted on 125th Street. We played all the high spots in the country in the United States. But did you know, we never played at one of the big hotels in New York? Did you

know we never -- we played all the theaters, all the big theaters. But we never played on location at a hotel in New York during the career of Duke Ellington, when he started until he died. But we played them every other country, every other state and city in the world. But New York, our home base, we never played it. We never, never, never played them. How ironic can you get? We never played it.

Played the ballrooms, we played the theaters. We were the first colored band to play the Palace Theater which was the performer's heaven. That was a performer's heaven. When he played the Palace in New York he was at the top of the heap. Like the Palladium in London. We played that. First ones; we played the premier of Maurice Chevalier at the Fulton Theater when he come to America. But we never played an engagement at a big, fine white hotel in New York.

They'd reach out and get Guy Lombardo and anybody but the soul brothers never got it. You'd better believe it, baby. You ask me, I'll tell you. Because I revert back to what I say, I was there. I was behind the Cotton Curtain. I was behind the Cotton Curtain. That's what we called it. I was there.
I know one time we did a broadcast with -- is his name Orson Welles?
Yeah, Orson Welles.
The big star?
Yeah, director. Made movies.

Yeah, it was radio then. Wasn't no TV. We did this thing. We had Hall Johnson's choir, one of the famous colored choirs in the world, famous. Ethel Waters, our band. We done this program for Mobil Oil. The Southern stations cut it off because we was colored. And it was one of the damnedest things you ever heard in your life because here's this big choir that sang. Oh, they sang, man. Something else. They were fabulous. Ethel Waters was at her peak then. She was beautiful. And our band put the icing on the cake. But they wouldn't play it on one of those Southern stations. I never got over it.

Mobil Oil. They wouldn't even play our records down home. Uh-uh. They play race records. Now, these other slobs, they'd play them all over the country and they ain't saying nothing. Country and Western, Nashville.
Do you have any relatives in the South? You have any Southern relatives?

I don't recognize them, no. My mother was -- this is true. My mother was born in South Carolina, my father was born in North Carolina. The furthest I've ever been South at that time, I was born in Jersey. My sisters was born in Jersey. My brother was born in Jersey. All I knew, South Jersey. And I was scared of that.
(Laughter.)
You'd better believe it.

My grandparents left me some property down in North Carolina. Give it to somebody, I don't want it. Not me. No, no, I'm telling you, man, ain't no way. I don't know who got it. I wouldn't care less. You'd better believe it. Because I don't know, intuition, you call it intuition, I was always sceptical about them cats below the Mason-Dixon. Scared. I wasn't scared; I just didn't want to have nothing to do with them.
Barney, here's a funny story. Cut that.
(Recording interruption.)
Now we've switched, we're going to talk about Los Angeles. Go ahead.
We went out, the first time I went to Los Angeles we went out to make the picture --
Those movies?
Check and Double Check.
And Murder at the Vanities.

And Murder at the Vanities. And I went out there, man, sun was shining, everybody out there playing that miniature golf and everything was beautiful. So I said, boy, this is -- I called New York, I called my father. I say, "This is it. Sell the house and come out here." He say, "No." Man, we was in the hotel, the Dunbar. You remember the Dunbar Hotel on Central Avenue?
Yeah, at about 42nd.

Yeah, we were in the Dunbar. We were living there. So the hotel got to shaking one morning, early. I was downstairs in the shooting gallery, because (inaudible) down there getting an eye-opener. Man, one of them light tremors -- one of them heavy tremors. Ray Nance got downstairs in the lobby of this hotel with only his shorts on. I said, "Man, where are you going?" He said, "Man, the world's coming to an end." I said, "Man, it's okay." Had to take a lot of people to talk to him, he was so scared. But I'm (inaudible) don't pay it no mind.

So we used to go out, the studio would send a driver for us. Come out -- because that's a long ways out to Hollywood from Central Avenue. We had to go out early. So we were riding around, riding around. And you know, the car stopped -- the bus stops in California, they sit on the side. So we were riding along and I'm sitting at the window and I lean out and just said to women going to work, "Hi, Sue."

Right away Duke say, "Man, that's a title for a song." And he wrote it. "Hi, Sue." We recorded it. "Hi, Sue." That's right. So we get on the set and we were making -- you know, we were making this Amos and Andy thing first and they were --(Freeman and) Gosden and them were very good friends of mine. And so they said, "Hey, Sonny, how you feel?" I said, "Terrible". They said, "Come on, Man, we have a little taste on after work."
What were some songs from that picture?
I don't remember.
I don't think they had a hit song in that picture. But we made the picture anyhow. They were very nice. So then we go from there to Murder at the Vanities, you know. So I think I told you about that.
Right. You know what? You probably -- the incidents you remember with Ray Nance probably happened when you all were making "Cabin in the Sky."
With Ethel Waters.
Right.
Ethel Waters.
Yeah, because Nance wasn't in the band when you all made Murder at the Vanities (Phonetic). He hadn't joined the band yet.

No. Buck and Bubbles was in Cabin in the Sky. Ethel Waters, the hit song from that picture was (humming). She sang -- what was the name of that? "Cabin in the Sky." Yeah, beautiful. She always used it to the day she died. That was one of her main songs. Nobody could sing it like --
What kind of a person was she?
Beautiful. Very -- Ethel Waters was -- I knew her from working with her at the Cotton Club. Because I used to get a little extra taste on the side for talking to

her. She used to sing, 'I'm going to sit down/-- ain't going to give it away, I'm going to sit down on it.' And I used to, She liked it so much she would always put something in my pockets, a little taste in my -- because I wouldn't do nothing, I wouldn't say hello if I didn't get some money.
(Laughter.)

But me and her was like that. Great. She was going with Eddie Mallory then, you know. Very hard to get along with. She didn't take no back -- took off of nobody. I got along good with her because when she started to get tight with me, I would dummy up on her and not say nothing. In the songs, when she was going to say -- I'd say nothing. It would break her heart. 'Why do you talk to them?' I'd say, 'Well, I didn't figure you was talking to me.' Then we'd go right back, catch up, that money going right on.
She was beautiful. But you had to know how --
: Had to know how to handle her?

Yeah, handle her and stay a little ahead of her. But she was very, very beautiful. And she sang 'Stormy Weather' like nobody. But Ivie could sing it like her. I don't know who sang it the best, her or Ivie.

But Duke used to hate that song. And we were the first ones to play it, coast to coast. Because the guy wrote it, he brought it up there and we played it on the broadcast, coast to coast. And she sang it. So when we left there, Ivie picked
it up and sang it. Beautiful. But everytime she sang it, it rained.
(Laughter.)

Everytime Ivie sang "Stormy Weather," it rained. And I hated that song, Duke hated that song. I'd say, "Well, why do you play it?" And it was one of her biggest numbers so we did it to pacify her. I'd say, "Ivie, don't sing that song. Baby, I love you." I used to con her. Say, "It's one of my big numbers." I'd say, "What the hell, do you like rain?"
(Laughter.)

She sang it (inaudible) it rained. Everytime she sang that goddamned song with the band. No kidding. I'm not superstitious, I'm nothing like that. But I swear she sang it. And another thing. (Al) Hibbler was sitting with the band. Now we come to Atlanta, Georgia. Man, the place was crowded, packed and jammed. The colored could dance but the whites were spectators up in the galleries. White couldn't dance; colored could dance.

So everything is going along fine. Fine, fine. Got damn Hibbler, Hibbler say, "Hey, Duke, I want to sing my big one, sing the biggie, 'Don't Take Your Love Away From Me.'" Remember that song, "Don't Take Your Love Away from Me".
Now, I'm sitting right next to Duke at the piano. Hibbler was standing in front of me. Half the dance is over, everybody high, the patrons are high. This son of a
bitch got out there and sang, "Don't Take Your Love Away From Me." The cats start torching, beating on their women.
(Laughter.)

I say, "Man," one cat started shooting up in the air. Now, me and Duke, we got to tear out. Hibber said, "wait for me, Sonny!" I say, "Man, it's everybody for hisself." (Inaudible). I say, "Man, I got to get away." So that went over good. I say, "Hibb't, as long as you live," I told him and Duke, "As long as you live, don't ever sing that song." But he conned Duke. Goddamn if he don't sing it in Mobile, Alabama, somebody sang that song. The same goddamned thing happened. I say, "Man, don't sing that, you going to get us killed." But he sang it and they loved it.

If you sing it early, you know, before everybody is half high and they think about all the things their broad's done to them, then they come down. The fighting starts. I say, "Man, don't sing that goddamned song." There were two songs, "Stormy Weather" and that song, I never liked. Never liked them, never.
One musician I wanted to ask you about, too, that we mentioned before I started the interview, this guy, Seminole.
Oh, Seminole, oh, yeah.
said he was big Rex Stewart / in the twenties and thirties.
Oh, he was. You know, he was down in the Capital Palace. Willie (the Lion) had a band, six-piece band.
This was in the twenties?

'22. Capital Palace. It was a hangout for everybody in Harlem. So we Willie there and Lionel (?) had a band, Charlie Irvis was playing with him. Anyway, we'd hang out there. It was a hangout, me and Duke was hanging out together. We went down there and Duke -- they loved Duke.

So we was down there, all the piano players used to come down there, see what they could do. Lionel would say, "go out and play," Lionel washed them away, you know. So one night we're down there and in comes a little cat, raggedy shirt on, he looked like anything but a musician. So he say, "Mr. Smith, could I play one?" Jimmy Johnson, all us sitting down there drinking. So Lion looked at this cat, said, "All right, kid. You think you can cut it?" He said, "I don't know, I'll try."

This cat got up on the piano. I swear, the place is (crowded, illegible) started playing the roll, you know, roll. Man, Lion's mouth flew open, Jimmy Johnson's mouth flew open. Fats' mouth flew open, and Duke. Ain't never heard nothing like that. I'd never heard nothing like it. He played it and broke it up.
Lion said, "Hey, Kid, where you from" He said, "I'm
from Jersey." Or Lion said, "I'm from Jersey, too." And right off, he was in.

So the next night he come up with some xylophones and he played them xylophones just like he played the piano. Sharp. Really shouting. So Fats looked at me and looked at Lion, said, "This kid's really something." Better put him in the circus, this kid is a natural giant. He said, "Hey, kid, how you do that?" He showed them and right away he got in at the circle. But he could play. That's the first time I heard one guy cut. He cut Willie the Lion, James P, and all them piano players. He wiped them away. And he sat there. He didn't know how good he was because he had never been to the big time, you know.
Whatever happened to him?
I don't know. I really don't know. We became good friends, but I really don't know. I don't know whether he's living or whether he's dead.
Did he ever record?

No. Never recorded. Pathetic, they never recorded that guy. You know, it was hard unless you was in the circle. Clarence Williams had the recording things locked up. He wasn't in there, wasn't nothing happening, you know what I mean? He didn't have no reputation because didn't nobody know him. He's from some little old town over here in Jersey. Didn't nobody know who the hell he was. Pathetic, man. I wish they
could have got him. He was something else, though. I don't know whether he's living. I guess --
: He played the xylophone too, huh?
Out of this world. Out of this world.
: This was like before Red Norvo and those guys?
Oh, Red, no, ain't nobody ever heard of Hamp. Hamp was playing in California at Sebastian's Cotton Club. Louis was on trumpet, Hamp was playing drums, playing drums --
: Wasn't Les Hite's band, was it?
Les Hite's band. And Lawrence was playing trombone. Ain't ever heard of nobody -- that's the first time we heard Lawrence out there. At Sebastian's Cotton Club.
: This is when you all went out to make a movie?

Yeah. Then they got an engagement out there. We were featured band out there because of all the notoriety. And they was the house band. We used to play together, all of us. That's when Louis would make it 20, 30 of them notes, high notes, on some number he played. That's when Ray Nance stole it. He stole it. Louis would make 20, 30 counts, just like he's counting numbers. Every night, that was the highlight of broadcasting. Yeah, Frank Sebastian's
Cotton Club.
So was Seminole the first person you heard play the xylophone?
Oh, no.
No, I'm talking about playing the xylophone in a jazz band?
That's the first one I ever heard. They used to play them just ordinary. But I mean, swing them, make them shake. He was tough. He make them xylophones talk.
When you got to know him, what did you find out about his background?

I never divulge his background because I wasn't curious about it. You know, I'd just see a guy and I liked him, he didn't have to tell me no history of his life. I wasn't curious. I just knew he could play good and that was it. I never was curious, I want a guy to tell me his background. Because that was -- I thought I was infringing on his privacy and I always respected -- I never said anything. Because whether he was as drunk as bum, I just loved his talent, that's all. I never in my life -- even -- I never infringe on his background. That's his privacy.

How did -- we've gone around the world three or four times now. When the band -- when you all expanded the band and went into the Cotton Club, that was when the music was -- was that when Ellington Sound -- the big band,
that's when it started to develop, in the thirties?
Yeah.
That was when the music -- was that when the Ellington --

He had a chance to expand because he had a wider scope to work on. And Duke was very inquisitive. I used to tell him all the time, he'd write down his dreams, he'd dream something and write it down. He would try it, if it'd jell he'd keep it; no, out.

Then he began to think big thoughts at the Cotton Club. He started writing all that junk -- I shouldn't say junk, he started writing all that stuff and he went on from there. He never thought about writing compositions in the Kentucky Club. We just took stocks and changed them around and made them a little different, and sound different. Because all the bands of that time, they -- you know the publishers, the song publishers, would take a song and bring them to the club and you'd play them just like they're written. But special arrangements, they didn't have that. We were one of the first who had that, you know. We were first that had that.

We take them songs, popular songs, and make them different.
Did you ever meet Jelly Roll Morton?
I played with him. I recorded with Jelly for Clarence Williams. Jelly was a good friend of my piano
piano player, a light-skinned guy.
He was very involved in Creole too, being wasn't he?

Oh, man, them cats, cats from New Orleans, man, they used to way out talk about "I'm a Creole." But Jelly wasn't -- Jelly was just a nice guy. He never leaned on that. But Barney and Braud, man, "I'm a Creole."
What kind of guy -- I've heard that Jelly Roll Morton was like a very -- he was unpopular amongst a lot of guys because he was always telling them they were stealing his music.
Could be. He was very brilliant.
Very bitter?

Very brilliant. Yeah, Jelly was very brilliant. But outspoken. He was a light guy and he was outspoken. If he thought something was wrong, he'd voice it. Yeah, Jelly was a good friend of mine. I was in California when he died.
What did he think of Duke's band? Did he ever talk to you about the music Duke was making?
No, he admired what we were doing. You know, you must remember, we wasn't at the top of the heap, then.
You all were still coming up?
That's right. Still climbing.
When did you meet Morton?
I don't know.
Must have been in the mid-twenties?

Whether it was in New York or on the Coast. I think it was in New York. In Clarence William's office. I was so busy, I didn't know anybody by the name of Jelly Roll. I wasn't that deeply involved that this guy is that and this guy -- it wasn't like that amongst the colored musicians. It wasn't like that. They say, "Hey, Sonny, meet so and so." Okay, "Daddy, how are you? Fine, good knowing you."
Well, he wasn't outstanding with a great big spotlight in front of them's back then. Like them singers, them big singers. We just --
(Inaudible).

We'd meet them, "Hey, baby." And keep moving. We didn't stand and gape at them because they wasn't -- they all become real famous after they died. But in that particular era it wasn't like you'd see a guy and stand in awe of him, you know.
Well now, according to Rex Stewart, guys stood pretty much in awe of Louis Armstrong.

Well, Pops was always a front row leader. He was highly respected by everybody, you know. But he hung out with the guys. So the guys he hung out with like me and the rest of the guys, we never in awe of him. We just know,

that's our man. We don't stand and look at him, (unintelligible) Pop's just our man, until he died. He was Duke's man. Great admiration between them. I was a great admirer of the work he'd done but not in complete awe. I never saw a guy was in awe -- like I looked up and my mouth fly open, can't say anything. He's just another turkey, I don't know.
It was just -- maybe you had a lot of guys that would say, "Oh, that's Louis Armstrong over there."
Now, when you were with -- you and Morton were good friends?
Jelly?
Yes.
Yeah.
You all hung out together a lot?
We, me and Jelly, we had fun. Had a little social life, yeah.
Yeah, because he was a hustling cat, too.
Yeah, he know what's happening. He saw the smoke in the hills.
(Laughter.)
You know, he was a pool shark too?
I know he was. But we never played. He was a lady's man. a woman's man-- / Jelly, he -- I used to like the guy. I used to tell him, I'd say, "Hey, Man, you're just taking advantage

because you're lighter than I am." He'd say, "You're crazy." I'd lay it on him. He'd say, "Sonny, you're crazy." But we always enjoyed each other's company, you know. But it wasn't -- no one really hanged. Man, I was so busy running, me and Toby and Johnny was running crazy, man. You'd better believe it.
You ever meet Bessie Smith during those years?
I recorded a couple of times with her. But, I mean, she was very reserved. You know, she had a and like us guys, sidemen, we were sidemen. Like we'd play for her and that was it. Not socially.
I've read before that she had a gigantic sound she was making. Her sound was unusually big.

Big and blue. They ain't never caught up to her. I can name a lot of vocalists that these young turkeys never caught up--now, Coral (PHONETIC), the girl that died, she sang solo, solo singing. What's her name?-- Chicago. She did a concert with Duke. What's her name?
Was she from Chicago, the spiritual singer?
Yeah.
Oh, Mahalia Jackson.
Yeah. Beautiful. Yeah. These cats, these long-haired broads with a guitar, $3.00 guitar,

They try but it ain't there, baby. It's right. That's our heritage, don't you ever forget. Rhythm, music and dancing, that's our heritage. Don't ever let nobody sell me no soap that the Negroes heritage is picking cotton. Shit, I don't even wear cotton shirts. I wear (inaudible).
(Laughter.)

That's our heritage. You'd better believe it. They're still -- all this jive they're selling now is a fad. I can't realize -- there's no greater attribute than to be imitated. But it must be good. They're bad.
Do you think that the white musicians who were imitating the Negro musicians in the twenties and thirties were better imitators than the ones today?
Yeah, yeah. 100 percent better.
Who were some of the ones you met with that were the best imitators?

They could copy. They could copy note for note. They would go out and buy them records and study religiously. The only time they'd falter, when it comes to individual solos. Because the average colored musician, they couldn't write down how he'd think. Because the average writer would write a skeleton for a number and then make adaptions. Give me two choruses, give me four choruses. Then you would play how you felt. They couldn't write that. Even Duke, they couldn't write it.

He wanted to hear something very beautiful in one of his numbers, he'd write the skeleton and point to Johnny Holiday and say "Play it." And Johnny played the prettiest chorus. Lawrence, Carney all them sharps, Ben, all stars. But it wasn't like you say from top to bottom a sheet. Impossible. Because he would write his dream and then them guys would interpret his dream.
Well, after these guys would improvise on a record and the record would come out, did they play the same solo after that as the ones they played on the record?

No, similar. Not note for note. Similar. Because they always kept the same -- and a lot of the times we'd make a record and a lot of times when they'd come to the solo it would even be better than on the record. And Duke would say, why didn't you put that on the record? "I never thought of it." That's right. Ain't never thought of it.

When you're speaking of white musicians, when we first went to Europe in '33, I was riding in a cab. And heard them play one of our numbers and it sounded exactly like our band until it got to the solo. Individual solos, then I knew it was this guy -- what was his name? Jack Hylton. It was his band. And he had the band, he was a Paul Whiteman of Europe. I said, oh, no, that ain't our band. I spotted it right away.
Well, when you -- so Duke didn't

No, no. Duke kept his guys, when it come to a solo, very loose. Play it, but you could recognize it. Play it not too far out from it; they could play it. They'd play it. But he never chastized none of the guys. He'd say, "You got it", that's all. He would look at them and say, "Hey, you got it." And they played it. They played their version, their solo. He was playing his dreams but they were interpreting.
You know, one of the things that was really very interesting to me about Duke Ellington's band is in looking at photographs of the band, you know.
Oh, yeah.

Like I had noticed, in looking back at a lot of books, photographs of bands, that the Ellington band seemed like it had a greater variety of guys in it. What I mean is, when you look back in a book a lot of times you'll see a band, colored band, most of the guys in the band are dark or there'll be a band where most guys are light-skinned guys. But in this band you've got everybody.
Like a rainbow.
(Laughter.)
In other words, that was one of the things I noticed that was really unusual about the band. It
was like if he liked the way you played --

If Duke liked the way you played, he didn't care how you looked. That was it. He didn't care how you looked, he took talent. Duke always -- his god was talent. He could single out a guy who you would say, this cat can't play nothing. But he could see something in him. He was just a genius like that. He didn't care if a guy was light or dark. If he could play, he played.
Because you all had -- like you had Creoles in the band. You had West Indians, you had --
Puerto Ricans, Tizol, an old Puerto Rican. Yeah, we had everybody. And like I say, it was a family. We had Creoles, Puerto Ricans, Indians. Yeah.
(Laughter)
West Indians, don't leave them, out.
No, from the plains of South Dakota, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, my grandfather was one of them cats -- Sitting Bull, he shot arrows at Custer's camp. Busted by the camp, pow.
(Laughter.)

That's right. No, no, the only thing Duke kind of drew the line on, that's how we got Ivie, you see, May Alex, the girl I was telling you about, the singer, a very -- she come to New York and was a sensation. But she was a girl, you couldn't tell if she was white or colored.
Oh, yeah, you told me about that. That's why he had to get Ivy Anderson.
So, when we got to Chicago, to open this theater in Chicago --
You told me that.

On our way West -- I'm telling it again. Anyway, Irving Mills is our manager. He said, I like that May Alex. So Duke say, "What do you think, Man?" I say, "Man, we look like hell with somebody who looks like a white girl standing in front of our band.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
