MR. CROUCH: Tape 4, January 23, 400 Central Park West, apartment of Mr. William "Sonny" Greer.

Now, we talked about a lot of the people in the bands, worked with the bands. We talked about traveling to different countries and you've done a lot of different kinds of things. I wanted to get some of your recollections about some of the individuals in the bands who haven't been really written and talked about that much. Like Jimmy Blanton, for instance. What do you recall about him when he joined the band?

Well, Jimmy Blanton, the first time I heard him was in St. Louis. We were in St. Louis to play the Case Hotel the first time they ever had a colored band. And so the night before -- we had two days off so the night before I went out on the town, and Fate Marable had a lot of very good musicians played on his boat, you know. So him and I were real tight.

So he say, "I want you to come up here. There's a jam session tomorrow and my boys, some of them are going to be there." So I went up, and him and I, we sat down, just relaxing a little taste. He say, I got a bass player I want you to hear. So all right, I see this guy, young kid, nice looking boy. And he played -- two or three more bass players played before him. He come up there and all my life I'd never heard nobody like this guy. Never heard nobody
play bass like him. There were some good bass players, but like him, never.

And the reason he was so different and fantastic, his first instrument was a violin. He could sit down in the concert, symphony orchestra and play the lead violin. That's how good he was. And on that bass, it's hard -- it's not difficult; he done so many things.

So I rushed back to the hotel and got Duke. I said, 'Man, come and hear this kid play.' So Duke went up and Duke was amazed like I was because Duke could see farther, what he could do. And Duke say, 'I'm going to get him.' So we had Billy Taylor was our bass player then. So Duke went up to Jimmy and say, 'How would you like to open at the hotel with us?' He said, 'All right.' And Fate (UNINTELLIGIBLE) told him, 'Man, that's a chance of a lifetime.'

And sure enough, he opened up at the Case Hotel with us. And it's too much. Too much, because he had a lot of his solos he gave to Duke, and we just turned him loose. And he fit the band like a glove. All the guys loved him, he was that type of guy, you know. So Duke say -- Duke gave him a featured spot all the way through the band, individual solos, because different guys doing an engagement, they'd get some solos. They turned him loose and the house caved in. He's something else.
I heard some good bass players, Oscar Peterson --
Pettiford.
Pettiford. And the boy who played -- who plays with Merv Griffin now.
Ray Brown?
Ray Brown. I played with all them guys.
Milt Hinton?
Milt Hinton.
Walter Page?
Old "Big'un", he's something else. But this guy, he started a brand new innovation for bass players when they heard him, you know. He was something, man.
What was it that separated him from the rest of the bass players?

Well, I don't know. Well, you know, he could hear a horn or something play a different solo on his instrument, and he could turn around and play it on his bass. That's what separated him. A lot of records he'd play, you can detect a different trumpet player's solo or different guy's solo, he could do it right on the bass, you know. That's on the record. But he was the first one I heard play -- I don't think I'm wrong but he was the inspiration for Oscar, all them boys.
(Recording interruption.)
So you say he was --
I know it. They all know it.
Yeah, everybody's gone on record as saying --
Yeah, they know that. He's something else.
In fact, Mingus said -- I talked to a guy this morning that had worked with Mingus for a while --
Mingus was with us a while.
Mingus said the only bass player he couldn't cut was Blanton. He said none of the others mean nothing to him, as far as a challenge. But just after he had heard Blanton play --

Jimmy'd eat him up, man. I'd play with both of them, Charlie and Jimmy. Eat them up, without any sweat. He was -- man, I don't know. He was so great. And when he was with us everybody tried to lure him. No chance. He's something else.
Oh, a lot of guys were trying to steal him from the band?

Yeah. But Duke laid so much bread on him, not a chance. Then he loved everybody in the band. Especially Ben Webster, he loved Ben Webster. Ben would take him everywhere and show him off to people. Of course, Benny always had somewhere to go, you know, different sections, different clubs. And he'd sic Jimmy on them. Jimmy wasn't wild like me and Ben, me and Frog, (that was his nickname.) But

he was something else, man.
I remember -- I told you about that, the guys who tried to get him away from us in California, Wanted to marry his daughter.
No, you didn't tell me about that.

No? Man, this guy in California -- this thing isn't running, is it? I'll tell it to you. This guy in California, a very wealthy man, and he had a daughter, only child. She saw Jimmy at the Million Dollar Theater in L.A. Fell madly in love with him. Beautiful kid. And she told her father, he'd give her anything in the world she wants. She said, 'I want to marry him.' He said, 'If that's what you want, all right.'
He came and seen us and he was amazed at Jimmy, a fine looking kid and could play. So he comes and asks Jimmy out to dinner and things. And he told Jimmy, 'My daughter loves you. If you marry my daughter you'll never have to play this bass again in your life.' A millionaire, man. I'll put you in any kind of business you want, set you up for life.'
(Laughter)
Jimmy looked at the man and he said, 'No, I would never be happy if I couldn't play my bass.' He told me and Ben Webster that and we was looking at this beautiful kid, beautiful girl. And we said, 'Man, you must be stone crazy.' We and Ben told him, man, you must be losing your mind. You'd rather play the bass then live a life of ease? He say, 'I just love

playing." And that was it.
I said, "Man, find out if she's got a cousin."
(Laughter.)
She couldn't see nobody but him. Duke's eyes popped
out of his head. Natural vision. He said, "No." I never for-
give him. I said, "Man, you must be crazy."
Was this a colored woman or white woman?

Lily white. (You know,) at that time they
may have had some money but there wasn't no young -- this girl wasn't but
19 or 20 years old. A natural debutante. I said, "Pal, you're
crazy. I know you're crazy."

Oh, there's a lot of incidents come up here. We
go up -- you got Ben Webster down here?
Yeah.

I'll tell you after--- So many of them things
happened, you know. So many things happened that I don't think
I would put on tape.

Well, what were the circumstances, how
did Wellman Braud leave the band? I read a story once, I wanted
to find out from you if it was true.
You tell it.

I read a story once that somebody had
-- in "Ripley's Believe it or Not." They had in there that
Wellman Braud played the bass, slapped the bass faster than
anybody in the world.
We had that.
Yeah, and you pronounced his name Breau, right?
Breau.
Right. And he read this and he came up and after he read that he decided he wanted to be a leader or something like that and then he left the band then. Is that how you remember it?

No. He was tired of traveling. And he wanted to open a business in New York. In fact, he did. A poolroom in New York. And he just told Duke he was tired of traveling, he wanted to stay in New York. Never no argument. Never no big head or nothing.
But Ripley did write that. He wrote that and he said we were the only band that could play 24 hours on a stretch without repeating a tune. He said that. He printed it.
Was that true?
Yeah.
You all had over 24 hours of music you could play without repeating?
We could play 24 hours without repeating a number. Easy! 24 hours. We could play it. Ripley wrote that.
Now, when you had a repertoire this size, how did the guys -- did they memorize most of that music?

Two-thirds. Two thirds of it was memorized. Duke insisted on that. Because it mystified the average band, He wouldn't have to call 23 or 44 or different numbers, because when we started playing we would pay eight or 16 bars, just him and I and the bass. Anything. But when it got down near the last six bars, he would give them a tonic so the boys in the band would know what number we're playing. And he would turn around and give them that direct cue. So he would look at me and I would say to the guys, "we're rolling." That would make them ready. And after he played them bars, he would look up and man, that band would blast out there, that first one would kill you. (Laughter) Solid!---- would kill you.

That's how we -- and they never could understand. None of the bands'dn understand know what we were doing. Count does a little of it, you know. I noticed at the concert he would play not every number, but he would play a little--you know how Count Basie--tinkle it a little bit. And get up there and do like this and the band would shout. Well, he got that from Duke. Ain't no "one-two, one-two" you know, like Lawrence Welk or Woody Herman, all them bands.

Man, we played 16 bars and that was it. Sometimes just eight. The average guy wouldn't know what the hell he was playing until he'd give it to -- he'd say "watch it." And I'd turn around and holler back, "rolling". And that was it. And guys asked him a million times, how do you do that?

"I don't know." He'd shrug it off. But it was just a thing he picked up. I don't know where he picked it up from. But that's -- you never seen the one-two, one-two stomp off. If we stomp off when we're making a record. Because, I mean, in reality, stage or dance, that was it.
And we knew just what was happening.
So memorization was very, very important.
It was very important and it was necessary, you know.

Well, that also made it possible for some of those things like you were talking about, like for the band to start playing in the dark, too, without any -- sometimes you'd be playing and the spotlight might be on just one person.
Pinpoint, yeah.
Benny would be black, so you all weren't using those little music stands with the lights on them like they use today?
No. We had music stand but we didn't have a whole lot of lights strung out on them like they use. They knew what was happening. That's right. Something else.
Now what about -- how did you and Fate Marabel become friends?
Well, Fate was a big man, nice man, a ...Fate Marable was
night hawk. And he crossed me on one of my rampages. We were drinking and --
You mean when you first met him?
In St. Louis, yeah. Oh, the trumpet player introduced me to him before that. What is his name, one of his -- you know his name? Did you know any of the guys who played for Fate?
All I know was that Louis Armstrong played with him a certain time, I think Jabbo Smith played with him for a little while.
Who else? Another boy from New Orleans.
(Inaudible) Kid Thomas, Valentine?

No. But anyway, this trumpet player, me and him was in the bar and Fate come in and this boy, "Hey, Chief, come here, I want you to meet somebody." So that's how I met him. And he was such a pleasant guy from then on. He was my drinking man, because he used to ask me a lot of questions about the band and -- Fate Marable, him and his gin. We was close.
How did you like his band?

In fact, I'll tell you the truth. I never heard his band entirely. I never been around one of them riverboats. I was invited but I was always too busy. In fact, a lot of us, me and Duke, we never made it. We was so busy, you know.
But a lot of guys come from that band. A lot of
good ones come from that band. He always had guys that could play. I think Zutty played with him.
Yeah, I think he did for a while.
Yeah, I knew Zutty.
Yeah, you played with him for -- well, Zootie played--the style of drums he played was just a little bit before you came through?
He played strictly the New Orleans drum style.
Yeah, a lot of press rolls?
Yeah.

Well, you know, one of the things I wanted to ask you about your style of drumming, I forgot to ask you. Now, you know how like--(unintelligible). Most of the other drummers -- I listen to you a lot on records and most of the drummers would always play quarter notes for the bass player. You know, it would be boom, boom, boom, boom, boom (humming.) But I noticed on a lot of the records you play on, you're not playing that.
No, no. I played that sometimes but not continuously, you know. It depends on what we were playing, you know, that sort. You know, that's fine. A lot of guys got away from it now, you know.
Quarter notes?
Uh-huh. I don't know, man. I play
just usually with the piano. We played concerts like that.
You and Brooks Kerr?
Yeah. You know. And I don't know, intuition. Just a feel of it.
Well, did you get -- was it that you -- that sound, did you find it too repetitious or boring? Or you just heard something else you wanted to play?
No, it never bored me. I used to like to hear the guys play it.
No, I'm talking about for you. I'm not talking about them.
I don't know, it didn't bore me. I was so busy enjoying it, I never got bored, man.

Oh, no, I don't mean bored while you were playing. I'm talking about like -- you know, that's a distinctly different thing about your style of drumming and other drummers, you know, in theory. Because very rarely do you play that quarter note bass drum figure. I mean Chick Webb and a lot of other guys I've heard on records, you listen to them and they'd be playing a bass drum (humming). But you put on Duke Ellington's band, boomp, boomp, boomp ain't going on.
No.
And I was just trying to find out what --
I don't know.
You didn't remember?
No. Man, I don't know. Duke had so many ideas.
Did he suggest that you not play it all the time?

No, he never. He left -- he never told me to play this or that. He would leave it up to my intuition. He never -- I'd play. I'd just look, you know, I'd play along with the guys and I'd just feel different things that fit different guys.
Oh, so you would adapt what you were playing to whether or not you thought it would fit the guy that was playing?
Yeah. Or fit the number he was playing.
So if a particular guy was playing, was improvising at some point, you would -- if you thought that the bass drum figures went with his style of playing, and if they didn't you'd cancel?
Oh, yeah. Yeah, if it didn't go. You never hear that no more. Never hear that stuff no more.
Yeah, because, you know, Roy Haynes was telling me -- you know Roy Haynes?
Roy was a good pal of mine. Roy is my man.
Well, he told me that he thought you

were the first drummer that he thought kind of freed the drummer to play more different kinds of things. But he said Jo Jones was the first drummer you heard, instead of saying ("ting-tinka") ("tinka-ting") (humming) he played (humming). He turned the beat around a little bit. But then he told me, he said, man, "Sonny Greer, a lot of times he'll be playing and the bass player will be carrying the time, Sonny won't be carrying time, he'll be back there playing colors."

Yeah, that was it. You said the word. I colored them things, you know. Of course, it wasn't too hard on me to fall in for that because we had two bass players. We had two bass players that was holding the line. The only thing I was doing was coloring. Yeah, them cats would play something, I'd color it up so it sounds good.18): I know if it sounds good to me, it will sound good to everybody else. But not over exaggerate, I mean just color.

All the guys in the band liked it. Duke loved it. That's why he give me so much freedom, you know. Because he insisted that the rhythm section kept that level. Our brass, our reeds, all bands, two out of three bands, they start out here, when they go, they've done accelerated way up top. But where we started, we were right there. And that was difficult, you know.
A guy, naturally, playing a solo, he gets over energetic and he has a tendency to turn loose. You've got to hold
it. Right away he wants to take it up to the sky. But no, we have to hold him down.

Only thing, if the band -- like we were playing this theater with the band, we had the first show, say about 11:30. A lot of times them cats would stay out so late they're scared to go home. They come to the theater and go to sleep. Now, when they come downstairs Duke could tell, they're going to get a little sluggish, see. I stayed out with them but I had the theater; a valet when I get to/had the coffee and a little taste--coffee Royal, I had eight hours sleep by the first show and I ain't saw no bed. And them guys, at the first note I would take it up a little, just a little, not a whole lot, just a little to give them that inspiration. Duke knew it, none of the other guys -- say, "How did he start like us and don't feel tired like us?" I'd say, "Man, I had eight hours sleep before I come down here." I'd say, "Jonesy is my valet. He had that café royale for me. I'm wide awake."

Of course, after the first show, I've got to hit that cot, too, you know. I never let them get a chance to overtake me, tiredness overtake me. That's when Duke -- have you ever seen Duke play with his back to the audience?
Yeah.
Man, Duke used to stand up, they thought that was so cute, he'd stand up playing the piano and looking up at me and yawning. I'd say, "Come on here, daddy, let's go."
I had to keep hollering at him, talking to him, you know, keep him awake. Soon as we'd come off stage, he'd fall off and faint on the thing, man.
So in a certain way, as far as keeping the band going, you were more or less Ellington's right-hand man with the band? Musically and otherwise.
Yeah, I was. I was like a lieutenant to him. He could depend on me. All the way through, he could depend on me, all the way through.
Now, do you remember the recording? Do you remember working on a piece "Reminiscing in Tempo" that he dedicated to his mother? That long recording that was on four sides?
Yeah, we recorded that.
Remember that?
Yeah, I remember that. I made it.
But I mean, when you all went to record that, had the guys memorized the music? Or were they reading it?
No, when we recorded that, that was written out because it was so long. First time we recorded it. Well, eventually they memorized it.
Did you all play it in performance much?
Not -- we played in concerts. That was written strictly for concerts. You see, Duke wrote different numbers, every concert we played at Carnegie Hall, every year

we played there, a whole different program written. One segment -- half a segment was written, new composition that he would start a concert. But like -- what's this thing?..... Some guy asked, I think Brooksie played a solo last night, -- what did you ask me?
"Black, Brown and Beige"?
"Black, Brown and Beige."
You played a piece on "Come Sunday" or --

"Come Sunday," yeah. Because they had -- we had three girls singing in our band, Joya Sherrill --- quit then -- Ivie had in, Joya Sherrill, Marie Ellington, who later married Nat King Cole and Kay Davis, little girl who married a big lawyer in Chicago. She sang all them high notes. So they --
Betty Roche for a little while, too, didn't you?
Yeah, Betty joined us after Ivie got so sick she couldn't travel no more. She joined us. But Betty Roche never sang "Black Brown and Beige," you know.
Yes, she did. She sang --
Yes, she sang, "The blues ain't nothing but something." Yeah, Betty sang. Sang good, too. Oooee. Roche, she was something else.
Were you at the Carnegie Hall Concert that Benny Goodman did when he had -- I mean, did you go to any with Johnny Hodges and Lester Young and some other people were in
a jam session part of that 1938 concert you did? You didn't go to the concert hall?

No, I never went to it. I never went to it. Not that I didn't want to, but man, we stayed out of New York so much, we got to New York and no one had a chance to hear me. I was with all them bands playing, all them different guys. Wasn't no big thrill to me. A lot of people went, but I mean, I had a lot of other things to do besides that.
Well, what did you think about -- how did you like the white bands that were around at the time, did you think of Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw. What/ those guys?
Good.
You told me already about how you all slaughtered Goodman in Chicago---Fats Waller sat in with you all.

They were good. I like Tommy, I liked Tommy's band, I liked Glen Miller's band. And Woody had a good band. And what's the guy played with Bob Hope? Les Brown and his Band of Renown, I liked him. We played against him when he was still in school. I like them bands, they were good.

Collectively they were nice, but when you come to individual solos they didn't stack up to the soul brothers. Soul brothers would eat 'em up. Because they didn't think like we did. You see, rhythm is your heritage. That's us. And dancing, singing is our heritage.
But, you know, they didn't believe it. You'd have to put it in front of the eyes and they still didn't believe it. You know what I mean. Burn 'em down.

And we had to be -- you know, it was necessary. We had to be twice as good as them guys, you know. Now you do--- for recognition. You had to be twice as good. Had to be twice as good singing, twice as good dancing, playing the music. It goes to show you. They say no greater compliment in the world than to be imitated, you know. They're all imitating. All of them want to be soul, soul brothers. That's a big joke. If you ain't got no soul you sure ain't going to be down here with your soul gone, you ain't going to be sitting up here playing music. So that's stupid.
But like I tell you, man, Buster Bailey, Bushell -- you remember Garvin Bushell?
Uh-huh.

MR. GREER: He played all the lead instruments. But you think he's sitting with the philharmonic orchestra? No, because he's soul. But he was capable. I ain't seen the day, even the day that Benny Goodman could play like Buster Bailey. Buster ate him up like a turkey dinner. And Jimmy Hamilton, Barney. So, they splice him, the King of Swing. They'd carry him down. He playing the same thing out of Fletcher's book, years ago. Fletcher saved him. But right away they're going to make him the white champion.

Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Did you have -- at that time, too, do you think that's one of the reasons, given those kinds of pressures, are you saying that's one of the reasons why the guys -- like you were talking earlier about how the guys always are involved with dignity and having their presentations be real exact, everything on the button, guys look good, clean-shaven, you know, have their music down, have all their music memorized and everything, that that was a way of making sure that --

Yeah, well, you see, our manager, Irvin Mills, and Duke, insisted that we look good. We were the most dressed up band in the world. We did four or five shows a day, sometimes six, at a theater, each show we changed complete, from head to toe, uniforms. Everytime we played Carnegie Hall or important on that status (gible), He would have the tailor make us complete uniforms, complete shoes, everything. Because he always -- Irving Mills was a very shrewd man. And he knew appearance was half the battle. When you look good, and can play good, you can't miss.

Well, I've seen photographs of you all in Washington in the twenties before you all even met Irving Mills, and seen that you and Ellington and Hardwick were pretty sharp, about as sharp as you can get.
Sharp as a razor blade.
(Laughter.)

You see, when I went to school one of the main things my teacher, German lady, insisted on, now, a lot of you are going to be professional musicians. She'd say, "Well, let me tell you something." She's a German lady. "She'd say, appearance is half the battle. Always look good. If you look good and can play good, you can't miss."

What did she say that for, man. I became a clothes horse, you know. I was dressing sharp. That's one reason why I became a drummer. I saw this cat, Peg ? , man, he was a Rembrandt picture. He was tall and elegant. I said, "Man, I'd like to look like that." That was sharp as -- oeee, he was a gasser! I never seen -- sharp on the stage, off the stage. This cat, I said, yeah, that's it. I'm going to be like that one day, I'm going to be like that. And that was it.
So then when you all got the band together, it was like you and Ellington got guys to start being as conscious of --
Clothes conscious.
As much as you were.

Yeah, clothes conscious. And Leo Bernstein, the owner of the Kentucky Club, he wanted to see his bands dressed up. He'd say, "My band's the sharpest band in New York. And he keeps going down to the high priced and gets that -- all we had to tel him, "Man, I seen something down there that's too bad." He'd say, "Well, go get it, send the bill to
me."
Now, do you think that has something to do with the trend of all the bands getting so sharp after you all?
It could be. I couldn't definitely say that.
Well, the reason I asked is because when I was studying ble) the old band book pictures --
The Jimmie Lunceford band, all dressed, all the bands started looking after their uniform and appearance, you know.

Yeah, because like I saw some old pictures of bands and before the Ellington band, from what I could tell by these books, I don't know, most of the guys had like pinstripe suits on, or maybe a tuxedo. But like all those things, I started noticing you all started wearing tuxedos with like these satin lapels.

Full dress suit. We had a black full dress suit, we had a white full dress suit. We had different combinations. I'm quite certain we were the first one that had that. That's why Lady Mountbatten nicknamed us 'The Aristocrats of Jazz'. We lived the part. We were the part. And everybody was very conscientious of their appearance, you know.
You know, my mother told me when she was a teen, she was born in 1920, she was a teenager when the bands
used to come to Los Angeles and they used to meet the bands, she and the kids in her high school, they used to meet your -- at Union Station.
At the station. And we'd play, straight off to Central Avenue, around. Yeah, had them cars, the bands were playing. Just beautiful parties, you know.
Now, did you all -- were you all met at many train stations by people when you came into town?

Always. No matter what time of night it was or what time of day it was. / We'd come in the station, some local band would be at the station playing, and we'd come through the station playing. People would turn around, wonder what's going on. And they had their banners. All cities, that was it. That's the truth.

I remember one time we were on our way to California and we had a two hour lay-off in Denver. And a band met us at the station, pulled up to our Pullman. And the guy, what was his name, he was head of the union out there. He said, "You all hurry up and get dressed, we got a luncheon up in the station for you guys." Man, I got all dressed up in a grey outfit and man, my feet hurt me, I had a pair of rattlesnake bedroom slippers, man I'm all dressed to kill and Duke looked down, I had on these bedroom slippers. They were expensive. Duke said, "Hey, man, you got on bedroom slippers." I said, "Man, the way my feet are feeling, I'm lucky to be caught
barefoot. I said, "You want me here, don't you? If you don't, I can go right back in them." He said, oh, come on.

You know, there was a lot of funny incidents. And they had this band, all the band from the union guys in Colorado. They made up some jive band, playing in the station, making all that noise. Here's this guy, Ben Webster, hanging like a dog. Toby done high. But they made it and had a good time. Yeah.

And New Orleans, man. First time we went to New Orleans, had a station down there. They brought our baggage car and our Pullman there, that's how we traveled, right in the station. And man, them cats had cars lined up for three blocks, private cars then, bands. Band always -- what the hell was the name of them bands?
Oh, there's so many.

I know. They were there, had signs up, "Welcome Home Barney Bigard" Everybody's cousin, you know. Wellman Braud, Braud was there. And we'd heard so much about New Orleans, man. I'm the last one off the train. And don't you know, them cats knew me. Knew me. "Come on." And right away, I said, "I'm from here, too." I ain't never been there before in my life. And right away they call me in Creole, "cousin". I said, "Man."
And from the time we got there until the time we left, it was food, food, food. I never seen so much hospitality in my life. Everybody was inviting us out somewhere,

you know. Right away I fell in with a guy named Benjy. He had a big restuarant. He looked like a white guy. And I couldn't buy nothing at that restuarant, bar, couldn't buy nothing. And food galore. They'd say, "Hey, Sonny, what you like?" I said, "Man, I love hardshell crabs. Blue-clawed things, big ones." He said, "All right, I'm going to give you a present when you go." Actually, I forgot all about it. Man, the night we left, I come down to the station and the porter say, "Hey, Sonny, these guys brought you a present down there from a friend."
(End of side A as recorded.)
So you went in the train station and the reporter said what?

Here's a present from your friend. And here's a big bushel of crabs. I mean a bushel basket of crabs. And a case of beer. Now, can't nobody -- don't nobody know how to eat them crabs. Duke didn't know how to clean the crabs. Ivie didn't know nothing about cleaning those crabs. Barney knew and Toby knew. That's all. Man, we got to eating the crabs and drinking the beer. Now, this is about 3:00 o'clock in the morning. And man, Duke's standing up there with the rest of the band, he don't know what the hell to do with them, you know. So Duke says, "Hey, yeah, got you covered. So fast as Albert cleaned one of them crabs, Duke would have it or I would have it or Carné would have it, Johnny Hodges would
have it and I'd look around and the guys, everybody got crabs but me. I said, "Oh, no, I ain't going no further."

So I fixed about six or seven of them, you know, they were so big, for myself. Man, after they got the hang of it, them crabs didn't last a minute. And the beer. Now they wanted to help me eat mine. I said, no way. No, no, no way. But that was a lot of good -- so we left there. The reason we left so late in the morning, we had to play in Mobile, Alabama the next night. So we left. So Cootie's home is in Mobile, Alabama. We pulled into Mobile, Alabama, I think it was -- no we played someplace else, I forget where we played before we get to Mobile. I remember we got to Mobile about 3:00 o'clock in the morning. The station's packed, because that's Cootie's home.

And man, I was sleeping. I heard all this noise, I raised the little shade and saw all these people, I said, man, and everybody's hollering, "Cootie, Cootie." So Cootie come up. He was home, boy. So Duke came out, Duke put on a robe and came to the platform, hollered at us. I ain't never budged. So we played Mobile that night, packed, four, five thousand people. The white was spectators. You know, down there if the colored had the dance, the white people could come as spectators. But, you know, not dance. They were spectators.
So man, Duke or somebody say he liked watermelon.

Man, we came out of the dance and got two big ones, about this big, cooling in the ice, you know. Man, we sit out there and had a field day. Had a field day. All those things. But you know, the people -- it was so wonderful. Wonderful.

But as I say, we played everywhere. I never played in my hometown, Long Branch, New Jersey. My mother and father never heard me play. My two sisters never heard me play. My little brother heard me once. That's one thing I always felt sorry for, my parents never lived to hear me playing, my sisters never heard me. We played everywhere but they never hired great big bands down there, you know, I mean an outfit was so expensive. But they heard about us because my mother and father kept up with our progress, you know.
Oh, yeah, they got records, didn't they? They just never heard you play live, personally.
Only on the radio.
Heard you play on the radio?

Yeah. But in person, no. But she knew I was climbing, she knew I was climbing. And she used to read about the different progress of our band, you know. Man, she was so proud. The whole town was proud because I was the only one, white or colored, made the grade, from Long Branch. And anybody told my mother I would have went that far, never. Beyond expectations, you know.
When we got together, we had no idea, boy, up to no

no top. No way. Then after people started recognizing us, and our potentialities at the Kentucky Club, wasn't no looking back. You know, wasn't no looking back. And Duke was a dreamer. I often said -- guys would say, how did Duke come to write "Satin Doll" and "Mood Indigo" or "Sophisticated Lady"? I'd say, he's a dreamer, which he is. He could think of something and be sitting down in the dining room, kitchen, everywhere, and knock it down. Gone. That's right.
And all the guys, they have different ideas, they'd write them down or collaborate with Duke, and there, we're gone. So we always had fresh material.
Do you remember how the first Carnegie Hall Concert, "Black, Brown and Beige," how that came about?
No. How'd it come to be written?
No, no, how you all got the job. That was the first time you all had formally played there, 1943, Wait, I got it here. right? I think it was January. / Hold on a second. (Pause)
Now, concerning "Black, Brown and Beige," the performance of "Black, Brown and Beige," you played some -- performed it some places other than Carnegie Hall before you played the Carnegie Hall?

I think the first time we played that, we had this engagement to play with the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra, which was in my estimation one of the greatest orchestras, even more widely acclaimed than the Philharmonic in
New York. We played a place called 'Robin Hood Dell,' that's right.

leads me right-- I remember--my memory of this symphony orchestra played all of our tunes. We set in with the symphony orchestra. We were right in the middle of the symphony orchestra, 100 or so of us. And we played -- I don't know, I'm quite sure we played "Black, Brown and Beige." That's the first time Duke played it. Because the symphony orchestra was so enthused about this particular number, "Black, Brown and Beige." Of course, they played a lot of our different tunes, you know. And we had a field day, man. Can you imagine us sitting up there in the middle of this great big symphony, one of the best in the world that Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra. Don't let no one kid you. They were something else. They traveled all over the world. And this Robin Hood Dell, prettiest place, outdoors, youknow, in the summer, beautiful.

And the only thing Duke and I regretted, Duke and the boys regretted rather, nobody put it on tape or record. That was the greatest thing we ever played. The greatest. That was the greatest concert or the greatest thing we ever done. Everyone said it. And we had guys, because we recorded all the time. How they missed that, I'll never know. How they ever missed that I will never, never know.
They had a guest soloist, Ella Fitzgerald? It was either Ella Fitzgerald -- I'm sure it was Ella Fitzgerald or,
at that time, Sarah Vaughn.
Oh, yeah, because she had been working with Earl Hines at about that time, right?

She was singing like a mockingbird. I'm sure it was Sarah Vaughn. It wasn't Ella. Man, that was it. That thing, recording anybody -- nobody thought to record it. If that had been recorded, you could demand any amount of money you wanted for that, you know.
Was it broadcast?
No, no.
It wasn't broadcast, either?
No, uh-uh. Everybody slept it. It was really the Duke was -- he slept it, Irving Mills, our manager, slept it. And after it was all over we knew it should have been recorded.
You played the entire work, "Black, Brown and Beige," with the orchestra?
With the symphony orchestra. Can you imagine how that would sound, with all them violins and stuff? Man, "Come Sunday"-- and "Come Sunday" was in it.
Right.
Can you imagine them violins crying, huh? And Sarah Vaughn singing?
Yeah, because I remember when I first heard it on record, just that opening, (humming). Just that,
you know, because you play a thing on there, (humming) and when they come back with that (humming). Then it goes into something else, you know. But I know that must have been a pretty powerful --

Man, a hundred and some musicians and them strings, boy, when they played "Come Sunday," and Sarah was singing, you know, not no trills, just plain, natural singing. And she could go -- she didn't have all that frills. Just beautiful singing.
She just sang notes?
Notes.
No words? Did she have any words or did she just --
I don't recall, but I know it was pretty. And people sitting all on -- that's the prettiest place, man (of the Schuylkill River) the banks, man, the moon was shining. I don't know, man.
And then after that you all presented it in New York?
Yeah, we laid it on Carnegie Hall. We laid it smack, dab on them, man, killed them.
Now, wasn't it a terrible snowstorm that you all performed in?
That was the biggest blizzard New York had. Because my wife and my daughter was down. Couldn't no

cabs run. We were living up in the Bronx then. The only way we got home, a friend of mine who had one of them Army trucks, charged $1.00 a head, they were getting rough! That's the way we got home. It was a blizzard, man. It was one of them hard, hard, hard blizzards. I think a lot of people, they just kept the hall open all night long because the people couldn't get home.
Did many people turn out, anyway?
Oh, the whole hall, it was packed.
Oh, even with the blizzard it was packed?

Didn't mean a thing. Packed and jammed, hanging on the ceiling, chandeliers, you know. We was packed. Because when the concert -- the blizzard didn't start until after the concert started. Nobody thought -- like that was one of the big blizzards in New York. That's right. We laid that on them. We laid that on Carnegie Hall. And every year after that, the man say, you ought to come back, every year we'd come back. Come back with a different program. We would play -- Benny Goodman played, well, anytime he can play, he's going to play the same tunes. But everytime -- that's why the man liked it. We had a complete program, new. It wasn't something people heard before, and they knew that. They looked for that. Never disappointed.
You know, in California. I know one time we played Hollywood Bowl. You know, that's a big place, too. We played "Black, Brown and Beige,"
we closed down -- we shook them up. We played that near the end and after we played that we went to something sweet, you know. Either "Sophisticated Lady" or --
"I Let A Song Go Out of My Heart" (Inaudible) or one of those pretty tunes.
Yeah, but we closed the program with "Mood Indigo" or something like that. And we played this "Diminuendo" and "Crescendo". You've got a record of that?
Yes, sir.

We laid that on them to stir them up, you know. And Molly, bar the door, that was it. Yeah. But all our theater programs, we always closed it with "Mood Indigo." Stage blacked out, just big, pinpoint lights on trombones, clarinets, and Carnev, baritone. And I was singing way in the distance, high falsetto, obbligato.
Oh, right, you mentioned that. You mentioned that you also put that on them when you were in Europe in that white --
That's right. That's how we closed our act.
Yeah, you told me you put it on them in Europe.
And they'd never seen that. They would dim down, at the end of it, complete blackout. And man, you could hear a pin drop (inaudible). Lights went up, man, that was it.
Yeah, of course.
You saw the write-up, 'Amazing Ellington.'
Well, you know --
I gave you one, didn't I?
Yeah, I've got it right here. But what I had wanted to ask you about, the -- one of the people who very rarely gets talked about is Freddy Guy.

Yeah. You see, Duke and Freddy was -- he was a beautiful guy. And Freddy, out of the whole aggregation, whole band, Freddy was the sensible one. He didn't have no wild traits like the musicians, like us. He was a rock of Gibraltar, steady. And all he had to do was keep that time, on that guitar. That's all. The four fingers you were talking about, that was his job. There's no record or recollection of him playing the guitar like the solo guys play, now, All he had to do was play tempo. And he was like the Rock of Gibraltar. That was his job.

And he was the mainstay of the band, rock steady. That's right. He was a lady's man. Nice looking guy, lady's man. Him and Sweetie Brown, lady's men. But Duke, Duke would always -- he was with the guys night and day. That's right.
I was going to ask you, now you know -- do you recall how Ellington got that scar he had on his face? Like in Mercer's book --
What did Mercer say?
Well, Ellington had three or four stories. He had one in the book.
What did Duke say?
Oh, he gave three different stories. None of them had anything to do with any women.
No, the scar?
Yeah.
What'd he say, how he got that?
Well, he'd say, I think he said he fell down, he was shaving, I don't remember the stories. But --
That's wrong. That's wrong. Now, what did Mercer say?
Mercer says -- let me see, Mercer says it was done by a jealous woman.

No, it wasn't done by no jealous woman. Who done it, I don't recall now. No jealous woman did that to him. No way. And Mercer, Mercer was -- you know, me and my wife, we practically raised Mercer. Mercer was a kid. He don't -- I don't care what he wrote, he wasn't big enough to dig something like that. And I've never read his book but he lost a lot of friends when he wrote that book. I never heard it. Everybody in our club, Duke Ellington Jazz Society, put him down. I'd put him down, and my being like a father to him. My wife practically raised him. He never
was around our band that much. How can he write about our band, because he wasn't around us. No, he wasn't. He was off somewhere, in Juilliard School somewhere. He never was around there.
But you don't recall how Ellington actually got the cut?
No. That's so many years ago, I don't know. I really don't know.
I think Mercer said it had something to do with Ellington and some women.

No. I knew all the women Duke fooled with. None of them cut him. No, that's false. No way. He was like a brother to me, he knows Duke and I -- he'd tell you that. If he had a brother, it would be Sonny Greer.
Yeah, that's true. He said that many times. That's odd, you know, you don't recall that.
No, I would have recalled some incident like that. I would have been there.
But, I mean, that's quite a large cut he had, it wasn't a small --
I can't verify how it happened but as far as I know, like I say, I don't know.
Now, I'm going to turn the tape recorder off because I don't want to read you this version of how you left the band. I want to see what you think, find out whether
it's correct.
(Recording interruption.)
Okay, I just read Mr. Greer the version of his leaving the band, that Derek Jewell (illegible) relates in his book, "Portrait of Duke Ellington".
The reason I left the band, when I come back to New York from Europe --

Right. My wife was (unintelligible), you know. So it was a toss up between I stay with my wife and the band. Naturally, I stayed with my wife. We were good friends until he died. You know, Duke -- I didn't have to ask Duke for no money. Duke was never -- there's one word I say for Duke, the word "no", he didn't use that. The guys will verify if you ever was to ask someone, no matter what money they want, he would never say no. No matter the amount of money, he didn't know how to say no, because they were his family, the band. That was his first love. And the guy, he never was a man that valued money above everything else. You understand? And the guys could go to Duke and any amount of money that was necessary, they could get it.

Well, now Norman Granz says, they also quote Norman Granz as saving, "Sure, I pulled Johnny and the others out of the band. I'd been very close to him ever since 1941 when "Jump For Joy" was in Los Angeles. I was doing my

first jam sessions out there. I used him on jam sessions and from time to time after the war I was in at Duke's band concerts. I felt Johnny was kept down in the band. I wanted to record him outside the Ellington context, and that's why he and the others came out. Harry Carney almost came too, but he was afraid to quit, and anyway, we didn't need him. Johnny's band had one big hit, it was 'Castle Rock', which was like a Louis Jordan thing with no singing. After a time Greer didn't want to travel so we used Sam Woodyard (PHONETIC) on drums and Aaron Bell (PHONETIC) on bass. It was a good band."
So now according to him, he pulled you all out of the band.

No, no way. How the hell could he pull us out of the band? No, he didn't pull us out of no band. Never. The way -- the first time -- they wanted Duke just to go to Europe on something they had over there. So he went and the only one he take with him was Ray Nance, that's all. And one of the singers, Joy Sherrill. So Billy stayed home, Johnny, and Lawrence Brown and I forget who, it was somebody on bass who -- who the hell played bass with us?
Aaron Belle?
No, no. I think it was Jimmy Blanton's cousin, what's his name. Bass player.
Okay, we can get that.
Well, anyway, we had a five or six piece

band, it would play (unintelligible). People went crazy. We played the Apollo up here, you know, cabaret, club...., had Tyree on the xylophone, we had a tough band. We were something else. So when Duke come back and he heard it he said, oh, no, you know. So some of the guys went back with him, you know. But I had made up my mind I wasn't traveling because it was more important that I be here with my wife.
We never -- we parted friends.
So Norman Granz wasn't connected with it?

No way. Norman Granz, he may have tried to pull somebody, but he didn't have that influence to do that. Because the guys may have played, recorded with him or something like that. But travel with him? No way. No way.
Now, those guys were out of the band for about three years, though.
Who?

Johnny Hodges. Johnny Hodges was out of the band from about 1951 to about 1954. And he replaced him with Willie Smith. And Lawrence Brown was out a little bit longer than that, I think. He came in much later.

I was out, '52. I don't recall. I don't recall when he left or why they left or what it was all about. Because, I don't know, I don't remember. I really don't remember. I couldn't be quoted as saying nothing like that. No way.
Well now, tell me about Billy Strayhorn,
That's one person we haven't talked about.

Billy? Ain't nothing I can tell you about Sweetpea. That's his name, his nickname. Because he was a guy that everybody, all the guys loved him. All the ladies idolized him because he was tiny and all the ladies wanted to mother him. I never saw a little man like that, could go up and stay all night long and cabaret all night long, sick all night long and walk the chuck line. He was amazing. He got me so I hated to look at him. I used to say, man, how you do that? And he would laugh. He would laugh. And Duke loved this guy. We loved him, I loved him. Everybody in the band, we idolized him.
You know when he first came in the band? Not the year, I mean, came in about the late thirties, wasn't it, about 1938 when you all did that piece (humming).
"Something to Live for".
Right. I think -- when did he come in the band? He came in the band -- let's see, Ellington's father was still -- alive.

Yeah, Uncle Ed. That's what we called him. He used to say, 'Will you ladies join me?' Boy, he was loved. The guys in the band loved -- when they saw him coming, the first thing he'd say, "Would you ladies join me?" Oh, he was something else.
When did he come up to New York? Ellington's father?
After we got settled in the Kentucky Club. He come up and he used to make a lot of trips with us, too.
Oh, he used to travel with the band a lot?
He traveled with us like to Chicago and California. He was beautiful. He was something else. Yeah, he was something else, man.
Do you remember when he first came up?
No.
But he traveled with you?

He didn't travel -- he made trips to visit us. He never did continuous travel with us. He liked big cities. He'd come and stay with us and go back, just on a visit, you know. He never traveled all them different places. No way.
No, I didn't mean a lot. I just meant now and then.
He would visit us in California, Chicago, Ohio and different places like that.
So you remember that when he came, when Stravhorn came into the band, did the music change a lot after Stravhorn came or did it change a little bit?

Did we change our style? No. No, he just added things to it. We never changed our style. No, it was too big a gamble, we never changed our style. But we played a lot of Billy's ideas because fit right in with our band.
But we changed our style never, never. No. Him and Duke would collaborate on a lot of numbers but the style was right there. Billy fell right in, the style was right there.
Only thing Billy changed was our theme song, "Take the A Train."
Yeah, because the old one used to was "East St. Louis --

Two classics. You got a record of that? Oh, yes, that was a classic. When them cats heard that, they know we was coming through. I don't know, I couldn't fall in love with "A Train" because it was just ordinary. But that "East St. Louis Toodle-oo", we were saying something. That was that growl, that's thunder and lightning, man. I don't know, I really to this day don't know why we didn't keep that. That was one of the brilliant things he ever wrote. Bubber Miley named that. "East St. Louis Toodle-oo"

Well, I remember reading something where Ellington said and later Rex Stewart himself said that in those days, the twenties, that each -- that the music really had a specific meaning, that a given tune would really be a picture of a given thing.
That's right.
You know, (it turned----) it got different later. But he said in those years, like Duke said, Ellington said he remembered there was some cleaners you all
passed called Olewando's (PHONETIC) or something like that. And everytime you guys would pass this cleaners they'd go "Olewando," or something.
Yeah.

I don't remember how it went. But he was saying sometimes Miley would come in and he would say, now, this is this guy walking down the street like this, and pick up the horn and he'd play that and then you might say, this is him falling out of bed, or whatever it would be, it would be something where the guys would actually put together a portrait of something in sounds. Is that close to the way it was happening in those years?
Yeah, that's right.
The guy said when Strayhorn came in the band he was just welcomed with open arms.
Oh, yeah, Sweetpea, everybody loved that cat, man.

Did you all only use that singer Jean Eldridge, on that one piece, "Something to Live For" or did you all work with her -- you know the one who sings with that little, funny voice? On the first verse of "Something to Live For". Remember, she's got that voice like (humming). She's got that kind of -- you know, the way she had her voice was kind of --
Did she make that recording?
Yeah, she's the one that made that one.
She wasn't with us too long.
Just for that? Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. How did Ellington strike up on the idea of using two bass players?

I don't know. One of his dreams. He was the first one to do that. How he did it, I do not know. I look around and I see two bass players, good ones. He never had no turkey(?) but they didn't conflict with each other. How he got that idea for using two basses, I never know.
Now, what about Freddy Jenkins? We didn't ask you that.

Freddy? Posey? . Man, Freddy Jenkins was a master showman. He played that trumpet left-handed, he idolized Louis Armstrong. The first time he heard Louis, when he went to California to make the picture and we went out to Sebastian's Cotton Club, Louis was playing out there with Les Hite, Lionel was on the drums, Hamp was on the drums.
